(b) The operator mutation would make lacZ turn on all the time, but I'm not sure if that counts as cis or trans-acting.
(c) Skipped.
(d) Alternative splicing is probably the answer, since different exons could be used in each cell type.

(a) Condition 1: low expression, since glucose being present triggers CAP to bind strongly and enhance transcription, but the lack of lactose means the repressor is still bound at the operator, blocking things overall. Condition 2: low-to-moderate expression; here glucose activates CAP even more, but the repressor is now released by allolactose, so we'd expect this condition to actually have the highest transcription rate. Condition 3: very low, since there's no lactose to release the repressor, even though glucose being absent lowers CAP activation somewhat. Condition 4: high expression because lactose is present (repressor released) and glucose is absent, deactivating CAP so RNA polymerase can access the promoter without competition.
(b) With the operator mutation, the repressor can never bind, so lacZ is expressed constitutively in every condition. This is a trans-acting mutation because it directly changes how much protein product (beta-galactosidase) is made, and trans-acting mutations are ones that affect the amount of gene product produced.
(c) Eukaryotic genes are regulated by nuclear compartmentalization, chromatin packaging with histones, and enhancers that can act at a distance via DNA looping, none of which are found in prokaryotic gene regulation like the lac operon.
(d) The most likely explanation is that liver and pancreatic cells have accumulated slightly different mutations over the course of development, since actively dividing tissues can acquire cell-type-specific DNA changes that would explain why the mRNA transcribed differs between the two tissues even though we call the DNA sequence 'the same' at a broad level.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Data analysis: mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm (1976) to 10.07 mm (1978), a shift of ~0.65 mm. This is directional selection toward deeper beaks. Four components: (1) Variation — natural heritable variation in beak depth existed in the 1976 population (beak depth is a heritable polygenic trait with continuous variation); (2) Selective agent — the 1977 drought depleted small soft seeds, leaving only large hard seeds available; birds with larger/deeper beaks had a survival advantage because they could crack large hard seeds; (3) Differential survival — only 85/642 birds survived (13%); survivors had significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population (9.42 mm) — evidence that large beaks conferred survival advantage; (4) Heritability — beak depth is heritable (genetic basis); surviving birds passed their deeper-beak alleles to offspring → 1978 post-drought population showed larger mean beak depth than 1976. Award 1 pt for correct data description (direction and evidence) + 1 pt for addressing at least 3 of the 4 evolutionary mechanism components.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Analyze beak depth data and explain the mechanism of natural selection — variation, selective agent, differential survival, heritability.
rubric.minimum_fix: Beak depth increased ~0.65mm from 1976 to 1978 due to directional selection: drought eliminated small seeds → only birds with deep beaks could crack large seeds → differential survival (only 13% survived, with larger mean beak depth) → heritable deep-beak alleles passed to offspring → population mean shifted.

rubric.evidence_requirements: p = 0.6 (freq D), q = 0.4 (freq d). p + q = 1.0 ✓. Expected H-W genotype frequencies: p² = (0.6)² = 0.36 (DD); 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48 (Dd); q² = (0.4)² = 0.16 (dd). Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. Comparison: DD observed (0.40) > expected (0.36); Dd observed (0.42) < expected (0.48); dd observed (0.18) > expected (0.16). Deviations are present. To formally test, χ²: (0.40-0.36)²/0.36 + (0.42-0.48)²/0.48 + (0.18-0.16)²/0.16 = 0.0044/0.36 + 0.0036/0.48 + 0.0004/0.16 = 0.012 + 0.0075 + 0.0025 = 0.022. With df=1 (for 2-allele), critical value ~3.84. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 → fail to reject H-W equilibrium (deviations not significant). Conclusion: population is approximately in H-W equilibrium. 1 pt for correct expected frequencies; 1 pt for comparison to observed and correct conclusion.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using 1976 allele frequencies; show all calculations.
rubric.minimum_fix: Expected: DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16. Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. χ²=0.022 < 3.84 critical value → population does not significantly deviate from H-W equilibrium.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) After El Niño, small soft seeds became abundant → small beaks efficient for small soft seeds → directional selection toward SMALLER beaks (opposite direction from drought). OR: if both small and large seeds abundant → stabilizing selection on intermediate beak depth. Most defensible: directional selection toward smaller beaks because small seeds are now abundant and favored. Small-beaked birds can efficiently process abundant small seeds; large seeds may now be scarce; smaller beaks may require less energy to maintain. (ii) Not Lamarckian because: Lamarckian inheritance requires that traits acquired during an organism's lifetime are directly inherited by offspring (use/disuse + inheritance of acquired characteristics). In this case: birds did not develop smaller beaks during their lifetime because seeds got smaller. Rather, birds with pre-existing heritable variation in beak depth (small beaks) happened to have higher fitness in the new environment → differential reproduction → their alleles increased in frequency. The beak size change in the population is due to differential reproduction of pre-existing variants, not inheritance of acquired traits. 1 pt per sub-part.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify selection type after 1983 El Niño; explain why this is not Lamarckian.
rubric.minimum_fix: (i) Directional selection toward smaller beaks — El Niño brought small soft seeds, which small-beaked birds can exploit more efficiently. (ii) Not Lamarckian — birds did not shrink their own beaks in response to environment; rather, small-beaked individuals already in the population survived and reproduced more, passing their heritable alleles forward.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Competitive exclusion principle: two species with identical ecological niches (same resource requirements) cannot coexist indefinitely; the superior competitor will exclude the inferior. G. magnirostris is larger with a deeper beak — better competitor for large hard seeds. If medium ground finch and G. magnirostris compete for the same large hard seeds: G. magnirostris may outcompete and exclude G. fortis → G. fortis population declines or goes locally extinct on Daphne Major. Evolutionary coexistence outcome (any ONE of): (1) Character displacement — natural selection favors G. fortis individuals with beaks different from G. magnirostris (e.g., smaller beaks focusing on small seeds that G. magnirostris cannot exploit efficiently) → two species diverge in beak size → resource partitioning → coexistence; (2) Niche differentiation — G. fortis specializes on different food resources (different seed types, different microhabitat); (3) Temporal partitioning — foraging at different times. Character displacement is the best-supported evolutionary mechanism. Note: actual documentation of character displacement in Galápagos finches is a classic case study. 1 pt for competitive exclusion definition + prediction; 1 pt for evolutionary coexistence mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain competitive exclusion; predict outcome for medium ground finch; describe an evolutionary coexistence outcome.
rubric.minimum_fix: Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist — G. magnirostris would outcompete G. fortis for large seeds → G. fortis may be excluded. Evolutionary coexistence: character displacement — selection favors G. fortis individuals with smaller beaks that exploit small seeds G. magnirostris cannot efficiently use → niche differentiation → stable coexistence.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Analyze the beak depth data from Table 1. Using evidence from the data, describe the change in the finch population's beak depth between 1976 and 1978, and explain the mechanism of natural selection responsible for this change. Address: the source of variation, the selective agent, differential survival, and heritability.

(b) Using the allele frequencies provided in Table 2, determine whether the medium ground finch population in 1976 was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the beak depth gene. Show all calculations. (Use p = frequency of allele D; q = frequency of allele d.)

(c) A 1983 El Niño event brought heavy rainfall to the Galápagos, dramatically increasing the abundance of small soft seeds. By 1984, mean beak depth had shifted back toward smaller values.
    (i) Identify the type of natural selection acting on beak depth after the 1983 El Niño, and explain why small beak depth was favored.
    (ii) Explain why this shift in beak depth does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance.

(d) The large ground finch (Geospiza magnirostris) arrived on Daphne Major Island after 1982 and occupies a similar ecological niche to the medium ground finch. Explain the concept of competitive exclusion and predict what might happen to the medium ground finch population as a result of G. magnirostris's arrival. Describe ONE possible evolutionary outcome for the medium ground finch population that would allow coexistence.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: Mean beak depth (mm) of the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major Island, Galápagos

Year | Mean beak depth (mm) | Sample size | Notes
1976 |        9.42          |    642      | Pre-drought
1977 |        9.96          |    85       | During drought (severe dry season)
1978 |       10.07          |    388      | Post-drought recovery

Drought conditions (1976-1977): Small soft seeds became scarce first; large hard seeds remained available longer. Birds with larger, deeper beaks could crack large seeds that smaller-beaked birds could not process.

Survival: 85 of 642 birds survived the drought. Mean beak depth of survivors = 9.96 mm (significantly larger than pre-drought mean of 9.42 mm).

Table 2: Allele frequencies for a beak depth quantitative trait locus (simplified diploid model)
Allele D (associated with deeper beaks): frequency = 0.6
Allele d (associated with shallower beaks): frequency = 0.4

Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 population (N=642):
DD: 0.40 | Dd: 0.42 | dd: 0.18

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a) Between 1976 and 1978, mean beak depth increased from 9.42 mm to 10.07 mm, a change of about 0.65 mm, reflecting directional selection toward deeper beaks. Beak depth is a heritable, polygenic trait that showed continuous variation in the 1976 population. The 1977 drought was the selective agent: it depleted small, soft seeds and left mostly large, hard seeds, which only birds with deeper, stronger beaks could crack efficiently. This caused differential survival -- only 85 of 642 birds survived, and the survivors had a significantly larger mean beak depth (9.96 mm) than the pre-drought population -- showing that deep beaks conferred a real survival advantage. Because beak depth is heritable, the surviving deep-beaked birds passed their alleles for larger beak depth to their offspring, shifting the 1978 population mean upward to 10.07 mm.
(b) With p (allele D) = 0.6 and q (allele d) = 0.4, expected Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are p^2 = 0.36 (DD), 2pq = 0.48 (Dd), and q^2 = 0.16 (dd). Observed frequencies were DD = 0.40, Dd = 0.42, dd = 0.18. Chi-square = (0.40-0.36)^2/0.36 + (0.42-0.48)^2/0.48 + (0.18-0.16)^2/0.16 = 0.012 + 0.0075 + 0.0025 = about 0.022. With 1 degree of freedom, the critical value is 3.84; since 0.022 is much less than 3.84, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, meaning the 1976 population's genotype frequencies do not significantly deviate from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
(c)(i) After the 1983 El Nino brought abundant small, soft seeds, directional selection favored smaller beak depth, because small-beaked birds could efficiently process the now-abundant small seeds while large-beaked birds no longer had as strong an advantage.
(ii) This is not Lamarckian inheritance because the birds did not develop smaller beaks during their own lifetimes in response to the new food supply; rather, heritable variation in beak depth already existed in the population, and birds that happened to have smaller beaks had higher survival and reproductive success under the new conditions, passing their alleles on more frequently -- this is differential reproduction of pre-existing variants, not the inheritance of a trait acquired during an individual's life.
(d) The competitive exclusion principle states that two species competing for the exact same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely -- the more efficient competitor will eventually exclude the other. Since G. magnirostris is larger and better able to crack large, hard seeds, it would likely outcompete the medium ground finch for that resource, potentially reducing or excluding the G. fortis population on Daphne Major. One possible evolutionary outcome allowing coexistence is character displacement: natural selection would favor G. fortis individuals with beak depths different from G. magnirostris (for example, smaller beaks suited to small seeds), causing the two species' beak depths to diverge over time and allowing resource partitioning and stable coexistence.

(a) The beak depth went up from 9.42 to 10.07 between 1976 and 1978 because of natural selection during the drought -- birds with bigger beaks survived better since they could eat the harder seeds, and they passed that trait on to their offspring.
(b) Expected: DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16. Observed: DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18. The chi-square comes out pretty small, so the population is basically in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
(c)(i) After El Nino, smaller beaks were favored because there were more small seeds around.
(ii) It's not Lamarckian because the birds didn't actually change their own beaks -- it was more about which birds survived and reproduced.
(d) Competitive exclusion means two species can't share the same niche forever, so G. magnirostris might push out the medium ground finch, but if the finches evolve to eat different food they could keep living together.

(a) Beak depth increased because of the drought -- birds with bigger beaks survived and passed on their genes, so the population average went up.
(b) Not sure how to actually run the chi-square test here, but the numbers seem close enough that it's probably fine.
(c)(i) Selection would probably favor bigger beaks again since El Nino changes the environment.
(ii) It's not Lamarckian because Lamarck's ideas aren't accepted in modern biology.
(d) Skipped.

(a) Between 1976 and 1978, average beak depth rose from 9.42 mm to 10.07 mm because the drought forced individual birds to develop deeper beaks over their lifetimes as they struggled to crack the larger, harder seeds that were available, and these acquired adaptations were then passed on to their offspring, causing the population average to increase.
(b) Using p=0.6 and q=0.4, expected frequencies are DD=0.36, Dd=0.48, dd=0.16, and observed are DD=0.40, Dd=0.42, dd=0.18, giving chi-square around 0.022. Since this chi-square value is less than the critical value of 3.84, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
(c)(i) After the 1983 El Nino, selection would favor birds with larger, deeper beaks again, since a wetter environment generally produces more overall seed biomass that birds need bigger beaks to process efficiently.
(ii) This is not Lamarckian inheritance because Lamarckian inheritance refers only to physical injuries or changes acquired during an organism's life, like a bird losing a toe, rather than dietary or behavioral adaptations, which can be passed on genetically.
(d) Competitive exclusion means that when two species compete for the same food, they eventually merge into a single hybrid species better adapted to share the resource, which is what would likely happen between G. magnirostris and the medium ground finch on Daphne Major.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) r = b - d = 0.28 - 0.11 = 0.17 per year. Exponential growth: N(t) = N₀ × e^(rt). N(3) = 980 × e^(0.17×3) = 980 × e^(0.51) = 980 × 1.665 = ~1,632 birds. Alternatively, using discrete: N(t) = N₀(1+r)^t = 980(1.17)³ = 980 × 1.602 = ~1,570 birds. Accept either method with correct setup. (ii) Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources, no competition, no predation, no disease — conditions that do not persist in nature. As population grows, resources (food, space, nesting sites) become limiting → per capita birth rate falls and/or per capita death rate rises → growth rate decelerates → population approaches carrying capacity. 1 pt for correct r calculation and population estimate with work shown; 1 pt for biological explanation of why exponential growth is unsustainable.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate r and predict population after 3 years; explain why exponential growth cannot continue.
rubric.minimum_fix: r = 0.17/year. N(3) ≈ 1,570–1,632 (accept range from discrete or continuous exponential). Exponential growth unsustainable because resources are finite; as population grows, food, space, and other resources become limiting, increasing death rate and/or decreasing birth rate.

rubric.evidence_requirements: K ≈ 1,200 birds. Evidence: from 1982 onward, the population stabilizes around 1,180–1,210 with no consistent upward or downward trend; it oscillates slightly around this value. This plateau is characteristic of a population at carrying capacity. Growth rate behavior approaching K: as N increases toward K, the logistic term (K-N)/K decreases toward 0 → dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K → growth rate falls. Maximum growth rate occurs at N = K/2 = ~600 birds (around 1974–1976 in the data). Growth rate approaches zero as population reaches K. Students may also describe: oscillation around K (overshoot and undershoot), which reflects real-world dynamics. 1 pt for K identification with evidence from table; 1 pt for correct description of decreasing growth rate as population approaches K.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify the carrying capacity from the data; describe population growth rate behavior as population approaches K.
rubric.minimum_fix: K ≈ 1,200 birds (population stabilizes 1982–1990 around this value, no sustained increase). As population approaches K, growth rate (dN/dt) decreases toward zero because (K-N)/K → 0; maximum growth rate was at N=K/2≈600.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Drought classification: DENSITY-INDEPENDENT. Justification: a drought reduces seed availability equally regardless of finch population size — it would kill the same proportion of birds whether there were 100 or 10,000. The effect is driven by climate (abiotic), not by the number of finches. Density-dependent explanations: (i) Food competition — as population size increases, more birds compete for the same seed resources → per capita food availability decreases → more birds starve or have reduced reproductive success → death rate rises or birth rate falls in proportion to population density. At low density, food is plentiful per bird; at high density, food is scarce per bird. (ii) Disease transmission — as population density increases, birds come into closer contact → pathogens spread more easily between individuals → transmission rate increases with density (follows mass-action kinetics: transmission ∝ density of susceptible × density of infected) → higher proportion of birds become infected at high density than at low density. 1 pt for density-independent classification with reasoning; 1 pt for both density-dependent mechanisms.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify drought as density-dependent or density-independent; explain food competition and disease as density-dependent.
rubric.minimum_fix: Drought = density-independent (abiotic factor that kills regardless of population density). Food competition is density-dependent: more birds → less food per bird → starvation increases with density. Disease is density-dependent: more birds → easier pathogen transmission → infection rate scales with density.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete experiment design: Hypothesis: Food availability, not predation, is the primary factor limiting K of G. fortis on Daphne Major (or reverse). Independent variable: food availability and/or predator presence (two factors to test). Dependent variable: finch population size / carrying capacity reached. Control group: unmanipulated island plots where food and predators are at natural levels. Experimental groups: Group 1 — food supplementation (add seed at regular intervals) while predators remain at natural levels; Group 2 — predator exclusion (wire enclosures excluding hawks/owls) with food at natural levels; Group 3 (optional) — food supplementation AND predator exclusion. Confounding variables: any 1 example. E.g., seasonal variation in seed production — control by running experiment across multiple seasons and using statistical controls; or habitat area differences between plots — control by using plots of equal area; or immigration/emigration — control by using enclosed populations or mark-recapture. Prediction consistent with hypothesis: if food is primary limit, K will be higher in Group 1 (food-supplemented) than control, but not in Group 2 (predator-excluded); if predation is primary limit, opposite pattern. Award 1 pt for complete experimental design (hypothesis, IV, DV, control, treatment); 1 pt for specific confounding variable with control method.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Design a controlled experiment to distinguish food availability from predation as the primary limiting factor.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypothesis: food availability is the primary limiting factor. IV: food supplementation vs. predator exclusion (experimental groups). DV: population size/carrying capacity. Control: unmanipulated plots. Experimental groups: (1) food added, natural predators; (2) predators excluded, natural food. Confound example: seasonal variation in seeds — control by running experiment across multiple complete years.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) In 1975, a survey of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major found 980 birds. The population had an annual birth rate (b) of 0.28 and an annual death rate (d) of 0.11.
    (i) Calculate the population's intrinsic rate of increase (r) and predict the population size after 3 years, assuming exponential growth. Show all work.
    (ii) Explain why exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely in a natural population.

(b) Table 1 shows finch population data from 1970–1990. Identify the approximate carrying capacity (K) of the Daphne Major finch population from the data, and explain the evidence you used to determine K. Describe what is happening to population growth rate as the population approaches K.

(c) In 1977, a drought reduced the finch population from approximately 1,200 to 85 individuals. Classify this event as a density-dependent or density-independent limiting factor, and justify your classification. Then explain how each of the following factors would limit the finch population in a DENSITY-DEPENDENT manner as the population grows: (i) food competition, (ii) disease transmission.

(d) Design a controlled experiment to determine whether food availability or predation is the primary limiting factor controlling the carrying capacity of the medium ground finch population on Daphne Major. Include: the hypothesis, independent variable, dependent variable, control group, experimental group(s), and at least one potential confounding variable and how you would control for it.
items.stimulus:

Year | Population Size
1970 |      300
1972 |      480
1974 |      750
1976 |      980
1977 |       85  (severe drought)
1978 |      380
1980 |      820
1982 |     1,180
1984 |     1,210
1986 |     1,195
1988 |     1,200
1990 |     1,205

Daphne Major is a small volcanic island (~0.34 km²) with limited food resources. Primary food sources: small and large seeds. Predators include: Galápagos hawk (rare), short-eared owl (occasional).

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) r = b - d = 0.28 - 0.11 = 0.17 per year. Using N(t) = N0 * e^(rt): N(3) = 980 * e^(0.17*3) = 980 * e^(0.51) = 980 * 1.665, or roughly 1,630 birds after 3 years.
(ii) Exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely because resources like food, nesting space, and water are finite. As the population grows, competition for these limited resources increases, causing the birth rate to fall and/or the death rate to rise, slowing the growth rate until the population approaches its carrying capacity.
(b) The carrying capacity is approximately 1,200 birds, based on the data showing the population stabilizing around 1,180-1,210 from 1982 through 1990 with no continued upward trend. As the population approaches K, the growth rate (dN/dt) decreases toward zero, since the logistic growth term (K-N)/K shrinks toward zero as N approaches K; the maximum growth rate actually occurred earlier, around N = K/2 (about 600 birds, roughly 1974-1976).
(c) The 1977 drought is a density-independent limiting factor because it reduced the finch population by the same proportion regardless of how many birds there were -- a climate event doesn't respond to population density, it just reduces resource availability across the board. In contrast, food competition is density-dependent: as population size increases, more birds compete for the same limited seed supply, so per capita food availability decreases and death rates rise (or reproduction falls) in proportion to how crowded the population is. Disease transmission is also density-dependent because as population density increases, individuals come into closer and more frequent contact, so pathogens spread more easily and a higher proportion of the population becomes infected.
(d) My hypothesis is that food availability, rather than predation, is the primary factor limiting the carrying capacity of the medium ground finch on Daphne Major. The independent variable would be the type of manipulation applied (food supplementation vs. predator exclusion), and the dependent variable would be the resulting finch population size/carrying capacity reached. I would use unmanipulated control plots with natural food and predator levels, and two experimental treatments: one with supplemental food provided at regular intervals (natural predator levels) and one with predators excluded via wire enclosures (natural food levels). A confounding variable would be seasonal variation in natural seed production between years; I would control for this by running the experiment over multiple full years and comparing patterns across all groups within the same time periods, so any seasonal effects would apply equally to all treatment groups.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Osmotic equilibrium: approximately 0.35–0.40 M sucrose (between 0.3 M where mass is nearly unchanged at +0.2% and 0.4 M where mass is slightly decreased at −0.2%). Interpolating: equilibrium is at approximately 0.35 M, where mass change = 0%. This concentration equals the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue — at this concentration, the water potential of the solution equals the water potential of the potato, so no net water movement. At 0.2 M sucrose: the solution is LESS concentrated than potato tissue (~0.35 M) → potato tissue has more negative water potential than the solution → water moves INTO the cells by osmosis. Potato cells gain water → cells become turgid (cell wall provides counter-pressure, preventing lysis). 1 pt for identifying equilibrium concentration with reasoning; 1 pt for correct direction of water movement at 0.2 M with explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Identify osmotic equilibrium concentration; explain water movement direction and cell state at 0.2 M.
rubric.minimum_fix: Equilibrium ≈ 0.35 M (where % mass change = 0). Potato tissue solute concentration ≈ 0.35 M. At 0.2 M: solution is hypotonic to potato → water moves INTO cells → cells become turgid/swell.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Water potential (Ψ): the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water; determines direction of water movement (water moves from high Ψ to low Ψ). Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Ψs (solute potential / osmotic potential): always ≤ 0 in solutions; becomes more negative as solute concentration increases; reflects the reduction in water potential due to dissolved solutes. Ψp (pressure potential / turgor pressure): can be positive (pressure from cell wall pushing back) or negative (tension in xylem); reflects the effect of physical pressure on water potential. (ii) At equilibrium with pure water (Ψwater = 0): Ψcell = 0. Ψ = Ψs + Ψp → 0 = −7.0 + Ψp → Ψp = +7.0 bars. This represents full turgor pressure — the cell wall is pushing back with +7.0 bars of pressure against the inward osmotic flow. The cell is fully turgid. 1 pt for correct definitions with equation; 1 pt for correct calculation and interpretation of Ψp = +7.0 bars as turgor pressure.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Define water potential and its components; calculate pressure potential at equilibrium in pure water.
rubric.minimum_fix: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; Ψs = solute potential (negative, due to solutes lowering water potential); Ψp = pressure potential (positive turgor or negative tension). At equilibrium: 0 = −7.0 + Ψp → Ψp = +7.0 bars = full turgor pressure (cell wall resisting inward water flow).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Hypotonic solution (lower solute than cell): Plant cell — water enters by osmosis → cell swells against the rigid cell wall → cell becomes turgid (firm); cell wall prevents bursting; this is the normal, healthy state for plant cells providing structural support. Animal cell (RBC) — water enters by osmosis → cell swells → if sufficiently hypotonic, cell may burst (lyse/cytolysis) because no cell wall provides resistance; RBCs lyse in pure water. (ii) Hypertonic solution (higher solute than cell): Plant cell — water leaves the cell by osmosis → cytoplasm shrinks → cell membrane pulls away from cell wall → plasmolysis; vacuole shrinks; plant wilts; if severe, cell dies. Animal cell (RBC) — water leaves by osmosis → cell shrinks → crenation (cell becomes spiky/star-shaped as membrane buckles). Key difference: plant cells have a cell wall that prevents lysis in hypotonic conditions; animal cells lack a cell wall and can lyse. 1 pt per correct comparison (hypotonic and hypertonic, with plant vs. animal distinction and correct terminology).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare plant cell and animal cell responses in hypotonic and hypertonic solutions.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypotonic: plant cell becomes turgid (cell wall prevents lysis); animal cell (RBC) swells and may lyse. Hypertonic: plant cell undergoes plasmolysis (membrane pulls away from wall); animal cell undergoes crenation (shrinkage/spiky shape).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Aquaporins facilitate osmosis by providing a hydrophilic channel for water molecules to cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer rapidly and selectively. They do not provide energy or actively pump water — they only lower the activation energy barrier for water movement through the membrane by creating a pore lined with hydrophilic amino acids through which water molecules pass in single file via hydrogen bonding. Water movement through aquaporins is still driven entirely by the water potential gradient (from high Ψ to low Ψ) — the thermodynamic driving force is unchanged; only the rate (permeability) is increased. This is facilitated diffusion, not active transport. (ii) In hypertonic solution: normal cell — aquaporins allow rapid net efflux of water → cell rapidly loses water → plasmolysis occurs quickly. Aquaporin-deleted cell — water can still cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion (lipid bilayer has some intrinsic water permeability), but much more slowly → plasmolysis occurs more slowly (or is attenuated in rate) but the eventual equilibrium state is the same (still loses water to hypertonic solution). The final equilibrium is driven by thermodynamics, not kinetics — aquaporins affect RATE of water loss, not direction or final equilibrium. 1 pt for correct passive mechanism explanation; 1 pt for predicting slower (not absent) water loss with correct reasoning.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how aquaporins facilitate osmosis without violating passive transport; predict effect of aquaporin deletion in hypertonic solution.
rubric.minimum_fix: Aquaporins provide hydrophilic pores for facilitated diffusion of water — they increase the rate of osmosis without changing its direction or thermodynamic driving force (water still moves from high to low Ψ; no energy input required). Aquaporin-deleted cell in hypertonic solution: loses water more slowly than normal cell (simple diffusion through bilayer is slower than facilitated transport), but eventually reaches same equilibrium state — same final plasmolysis, just slower.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) A student sets up the following experiment: potato (Solanum tuberosum) cylinders of equal mass are placed in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations for 24 hours. Mass change is recorded.
    (i) Using the data in Table 1, graph the percent mass change versus sucrose concentration (or describe the shape of the graph and label key points).
    (ii) Identify the sucrose concentration at which the potato tissue is in osmotic equilibrium with the surrounding solution. Explain what this concentration tells you about the solute concentration of the potato tissue.
    (iii) At the 0.2 M sucrose solution, predict and explain the direction of net water movement and the expected physical state of the potato cells.

(b) Water potential (Ψ) determines the direction of water movement. The water potential of the potato tissue in part (a) is −7.0 bars.
    (i) Define water potential and write the equation: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, defining each term.
    (ii) If the solute potential (Ψs) of the potato tissue is −7.0 bars and the potato is placed in pure water (Ψ = 0 bars, Ψp = 0), calculate the pressure potential (Ψp) at equilibrium. Explain what this value represents in the context of plant cell turgor.

(c) Compare the response of a plant cell and an animal cell (e.g., a red blood cell) placed in each of the following solutions. Use appropriate terminology (plasmolysis, crenation, lysis, turgor, etc.):
    (i) A hypotonic solution
    (ii) A hypertonic solution

(d) Aquaporins are membrane protein channels that facilitate the movement of water across cell membranes. A researcher finds that certain plant cells in a drought-stressed leaf can reduce water loss by decreasing aquaporin expression.
    (i) Explain the mechanism by which aquaporins facilitate water movement without violating the passive nature of osmosis.
    (ii) Predict the effect of aquaporin deletion on a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution, compared to a normal cell. Explain your prediction.

Note: All measurements at 22°C. Potato samples are from the same tuber.

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(ii) Osmotic equilibrium occurs at approximately 0.35 M sucrose, interpolating between 0.3 M (+0.2% mass change) and 0.4 M (-0.2% mass change), since this is where percent mass change crosses zero. This tells us the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue itself is approximately 0.35 M, because at this concentration the water potential of the surrounding solution equals the water potential of the potato cells, so there's no net water movement.
(iii) At 0.2 M sucrose, the solution is less concentrated than the potato tissue (~0.35 M), making it hypotonic relative to the potato. Water will move into the potato cells by osmosis, so we'd expect the potato cylinders to gain mass and the cells to become turgid, since the cell wall resists the resulting swelling.
(b)(i) Water potential (Psi) is a measure of the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure free water, and it determines the direction water will move -- water always moves from higher to lower water potential. Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p: Psi_s (solute potential) is always zero or negative and becomes more negative as solute concentration increases, while Psi_p (pressure potential) can be positive (turgor pressure pushing outward against a cell wall) or negative (tension, like in xylem).
(ii) At equilibrium with pure water (Psi_water = 0), Psi_cell must also equal 0. Using Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p: 0 = -7.0 + Psi_p, so Psi_p = +7.0 bars. This represents the full turgor pressure of the cell -- the rigid cell wall is pushing back with 7.0 bars of pressure, counteracting the inward pull of osmosis, and the cell is fully turgid.
(c)(i) In a hypotonic solution, a plant cell takes in water by osmosis and swells, but the rigid cell wall prevents it from bursting, so it becomes turgid -- the normal, healthy state for plant cells. An animal cell like a red blood cell also takes in water and swells, but without a wall to resist the pressure, it may burst (lyse) if the solution is sufficiently hypotonic.
(ii) In a hypertonic solution, a plant cell loses water by osmosis, causing the cytoplasm and membrane to shrink away from the rigid cell wall -- plasmolysis -- and the cell wilts. An animal cell in a hypertonic solution also loses water and shrinks, taking on a shriveled, spiky appearance called crenation, since it has no wall to maintain its shape.
(d)(i) Aquaporins are membrane channel proteins that create a hydrophilic pore through which water molecules can cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer much more rapidly than by simple diffusion. They don't use cellular energy or actively pump water against its gradient -- they simply provide a faster route for water to move down its existing water potential gradient, so this is still passive transport (facilitated diffusion), not active transport.
(ii) If aquaporins are deleted, a plant cell in a hypertonic solution would still lose water by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer, since the bilayer has some intrinsic permeability to water, so plasmolysis would still occur but at a much slower rate than in a normal cell. The final equilibrium state would ultimately be the same in both cells, since aquaporins affect only the rate of water movement, not its direction or the final thermodynamic equilibrium.

(b)(i) Water potential is basically a measure of how much water wants to move somewhere, and it's made up of the solute part and the pressure part.
(ii) If the potato is in pure water and its solute potential is -7.0, then the pressure potential ends up being +7.0, which is the turgor pressure pushing back.
(c) In a hypotonic solution, plant cells get turgid but animal cells might burst since they don't have a wall. In a hypertonic solution, plant cells shrink away from the wall (plasmolysis) and animal cells shrivel up (crenation).
(d) Aquaporins let water move through the membrane faster without needing energy, so it's still passive. If you get rid of them, the cell would lose water slower in a hypertonic solution but it would still eventually lose the same amount.

(iii) At 0.2 M sucrose, since this solution is hypertonic relative to the potato tissue's higher internal solute concentration, water would move out of the potato cells and they would become flaccid or start to plasmolyze.
(b)(i) Water potential is the measure of the concentration of solutes in a solution, and higher water potential means a more concentrated solution that will pull water toward it. Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p, where Psi_s reflects solute concentration and Psi_p reflects pressure.
(ii) At equilibrium in pure water, Psi_p should equal -7.0 bars to balance the solute potential of -7.0, since the two components need to add up to keep the cell in balance, meaning the cell wall is under tension rather than pushing outward.
(c) In a hypotonic solution, plant cells become turgid because the cell wall lets water in but prevents it from leaving again, while animal cells burst because their membrane is more permeable to water than a plant cell's membrane. In a hypertonic solution, plant cells undergo plasmolysis and animal cells undergo crenation.
(d) Aquaporins actively pump water molecules across the membrane against the concentration gradient when needed, which is what makes them so important during drought stress, since normal diffusion wouldn't be fast enough to keep the plant hydrated. Without aquaporins, a cell in a hypertonic solution would not lose any water at all, since simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer cannot transport water molecules across the membrane.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Efficiency, phytoplankton→zooplankton: 42/500 = 8.4%. Efficiency, zooplankton→small fish: 4.2/42 = 10.0%. (ii) Three ways energy is lost: (1) Cellular respiration — a large fraction of ingested energy is used for metabolic processes (maintenance, thermoregulation in endotherms, movement) and released as heat → not available to next trophic level; (2) Excretion/urine/feces — some ingested organic matter passes through digestive tract unabsorbed and is lost in feces (egestion); urea and other nitrogenous waste products contain energy not passed up; (3) Not all organisms are consumed — some organisms die without being eaten → energy enters the decomposer food chain rather than the grazing food chain; (4) Reproduction and growth allocation — some energy is stored in tissues not consumed by the next trophic level (bones, shells, woody tissue). (iii) Three trophic levels above phytoplankton to reach tuna (tertiary consumer): phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. Mass of phytoplankton needed: 50 kg ÷ (0.1)³ = 50 ÷ 0.001 = 50,000 kg. 1 pt for correct efficiency calculations; 1 pt for tuna calculation with at least one energy loss explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate ecological efficiency between trophic levels; explain why < 10%; calculate phytoplankton needed for 50 kg tuna.
rubric.minimum_fix: Phytoplankton→zooplankton: 42/500 = 8.4%. Zooplankton→small fish: 4.2/42 = 10%. Energy lost as heat (respiration), feces (not absorbed), organisms not consumed. 50 kg tuna requires 50,000 kg phytoplankton (50 ÷ 0.1³).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete pathway: (1) N₂ (atmosphere) → NH₃/NH₄⁺: Nitrogen fixation. Organisms: free-living bacteria (Azotobacter) or symbiotic bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules). Enzyme: nitrogenase. N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ → NH₄⁺ in soil. (2) NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻: Nitrification. Organisms: Nitrosomonas (NH₄⁺→NO₂⁻) and Nitrobacter (NO₂⁻→NO₃⁻). (3) NO₃⁻ or NH₄⁺ absorbed by plant roots (active transport, via nitrate transporters). (4) NO₃⁻ → NH₄⁺: Nitrate reduction in plant (by nitrate reductase, using NADH/NADPH). (5) NH₄⁺ incorporated into amino acids: NH₄⁺ + α-ketoglutarate → glutamate (GS-GOGAT pathway in chloroplast); glutamate → other amino acids via transamination. (6) Amino acids assembled into proteins by ribosomes in leaf cells. Award 1 pt for correctly naming nitrogen fixation and nitrification with organisms; 1 pt for plant uptake, nitrate reduction, and amino acid synthesis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Trace a nitrogen atom from atmospheric N₂ to protein in a plant leaf cell, naming steps, organisms, and chemical forms.
rubric.minimum_fix: N₂ → NH₄⁺ (nitrogen fixation, Rhizobium/Azotobacter, nitrogenase) → NO₃⁻ (nitrification, Nitrosomonas + Nitrobacter) → absorbed by roots → reduced to NH₄⁺ in plant → incorporated into glutamate (GS-GOGAT) → amino acids → protein.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) NPP = GPP − R. Tropical rainforest: 3300 − 2200 = 1100 g C/m²/yr. Temperate deciduous: 1200 − 800 = 400. Boreal forest: 700 − 500 = 200. Arctic tundra: 140 − 100 = 40. (ii) Tropical rainforest highest GPP despite smaller area than boreal because all four limiting factors are optimal: Light — year-round intense sunlight at low latitudes (near equator), no seasonal low-light winter; Temperature — warm year-round (25–30°C), optimal for enzyme function (photosynthesis enzymes); Water — high annual rainfall (2000+ mm), no water deficit limiting stomatal opening; Nutrient cycling — rapid decomposition in warm wet conditions means nutrients released quickly from dead organic matter and recycled rapidly into plant uptake. Boreal forests have seasonal darkness, cold temperatures (inhibit photosynthesis for months), frozen soil limiting nutrient access. 1 pt for all four NPP calculations correct; 1 pt for at least three of four explanatory factors for tropical GPP.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Calculate NPP for each biome; explain why tropical rainforest has highest GPP.
rubric.minimum_fix: NPP: Tropical=1100, Temperate=400, Boreal=200, Tundra=40 (g C/m²/yr). Tropical highest GPP: year-round intense sunlight (equatorial latitude), warm temperatures (optimal enzyme activity), high rainfall (no water deficit), rapid nutrient cycling (fast decomposition in warm-wet conditions).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Complete study design: Hypothesis: Removing the top predator (shark) from a coral reef reduces species diversity over 5 years. Measurements: (1) Species richness (number of species) and/or Shannon diversity index at the reef — baseline before shark removal and annually for 5 years. (2) Abundance of prey species (mesopredators like grouper, herbivores like parrotfish, urchins). (3) Coral cover percentage (as proxy for reef health). Method: Establish treatment reefs (sharks removed by fishing exclusion zones lifted or by simulated natural removal) and control reefs (sharks protected, same region). Survey via transect line/point counts at multiple sites annually. Statistical analysis: compare diversity metrics between treatment and control reefs over time, controlling for natural temporal variation. Determine result: if species richness/diversity index is significantly lower in shark-removed reefs than control reefs by year 5, prediction is supported. Limitation: any one of — (1) confounding variables (other human impacts, bleaching events) that could independently reduce diversity; (2) ethical/logistical challenges of actually removing sharks; (3) natural variation between reefs means differences may not be attributable to shark removal; (4) 5 years may be insufficient for cascade effects to be detectable. 1 pt for hypothesis + complete measurements + control/treatment structure; 1 pt for result determination criteria + specific limitation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Design a monitoring study to test the shark-removal prediction on coral reef species diversity.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hypothesis: shark removal reduces coral reef species diversity. Measurements: annual species richness/diversity index surveys (transect counts) on shark-removed vs. control reefs. Results: compare diversity between reefs over 5 years; support if treatment reefs significantly less diverse. Limitation: confounding variables (bleaching, human fishing) may independently affect diversity and cannot be controlled.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the food web diagram and biomass data provided:
    (i) Calculate the ecological efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers, and from primary consumers to secondary consumers. Show all calculations.
    (ii) Explain why ecological efficiency is rarely above 10%, describing at least THREE ways energy is lost between trophic levels.
    (iii) Calculate how many kilograms of phytoplankton (producers) would be needed to support the body mass of one 50 kg tuna (a tertiary consumer), assuming 10% ecological efficiency at each trophic level.

(b) Nitrogen is required for the synthesis of proteins and nucleic acids. Trace the pathway of a nitrogen atom from atmospheric N₂ to its incorporation into a protein in a plant's leaf cell. Name each transformation step, the organisms responsible, and the inorganic chemical form of nitrogen at each step.

(c) The data in Table 2 show the annual gross primary productivity (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (R) for four biomes.
    (i) Calculate the net primary productivity (NPP) for each biome.
    (ii) Explain why tropical rainforests have the highest GPP despite covering less total land area than boreal forests. Address light availability, temperature, water availability, and nutrient cycling.

(d) A researcher predicts that removing the top predator (a shark) from a coral reef food web will reduce species diversity in the reef community over the following 5 years. Design a monitoring study to test this prediction. Identify: the hypothesis, what measurements you would take, how you would determine the result, and one limitation of the study design.
items.stimulus:
Marine food web (simplified):
Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Small fish (anchovies) → Tuna

Annual productivity and biomass data:

Phytoplankton      |         500
Zooplankton        |          42
Small fish         |           4.2
Tuna               |           0.5

Table 2: Annual productivity of four biomes
Biome                 | GPP (g C/m²/yr) | R (g C/m²/yr)
Tropical rainforest   |    3,300         |   2,200
Temperate deciduous   |    1,200         |    800
Boreal forest (taiga) |     700          |    500
Arctic tundra         |     140          |    100

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) Efficiency from phytoplankton to zooplankton = 42/500 = 8.4%. Efficiency from zooplankton to small fish = 4.2/42 = 10.0%.
(ii) Ecological efficiency is rarely above 10% because a large fraction of the energy consumed at each trophic level is lost as heat through cellular respiration (metabolism, movement, thermoregulation); additional energy is lost through egestion, since undigested organic material is passed out as feces; and not every organism at a given trophic level is actually consumed by the next level -- many die and decompose instead, sending their energy into the decomposer food chain rather than up the grazing food chain.
(iii) To support a 50 kg tuna as a tertiary consumer (three transfers from phytoplankton, at 10% efficiency each): 50 / (0.1)^3 = 50 / 0.001 = 50,000 kg of phytoplankton would be required.
(b) Atmospheric N2 is converted to ammonium (NH4+) through nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria like Rhizobium (in root nodules) or free-living Azotobacter, using the enzyme nitrogenase. That ammonium is converted through nitrification, first to nitrite (NO2-) by Nitrosomonas and then to nitrate (NO3-) by Nitrobacter. Nitrate (or ammonium) is absorbed by plant roots and, if absorbed as nitrate, is reduced back to ammonium using nitrate reductase. That ammonium is incorporated into glutamate via the GS-GOGAT pathway, and glutamate's amino group is transferred to other molecules through transamination to build the full range of amino acids, which are assembled by ribosomes into proteins in the leaf cell.
(c)(i) NPP = GPP - R. Tropical rainforest: 3,300 - 2,200 = 1,100 g C/m^2/yr. Temperate deciduous: 1,200 - 800 = 400. Boreal forest: 700 - 500 = 200. Arctic tundra: 140 - 100 = 40.
(ii) Tropical rainforests have the highest GPP because all the major limiting factors for photosynthesis are optimal there: intense, consistent sunlight year-round near the equator, warm temperatures year-round that keep photosynthetic enzymes at their optimum rate, abundant rainfall that prevents water stress, and rapid nutrient cycling because warm, moist conditions speed up decomposition, quickly releasing nutrients back to actively growing plants.
(d) My hypothesis is that removing the top predator (shark) reduces species diversity on the coral reef over time. I would measure species richness and/or a Shannon diversity index via transect or point-count surveys at both shark-removed (treatment) reefs and shark-present (control) reefs, taking baseline measurements before removal and then annually for 5 years, along with abundance of key prey species and percent coral cover. I would determine the result by statistically comparing diversity metrics between treatment and control reefs -- if treatment reefs show significantly lower diversity by year 5, the prediction is supported. One limitation is that other confounding factors, such as coral bleaching events or unrelated fishing pressure, could independently reduce diversity on either reef type.

(a)(i) Efficiency from phytoplankton to zooplankton is 42/500, about 8%, and from zooplankton to fish is 4.2/42, about 10%.
(ii) Efficiency is low because energy gets lost as heat, in waste, and because not everything gets eaten.
(iii) You'd need 50,000 kg of phytoplankton to support a 50 kg tuna since it's 10% efficient at each step.
(b) Nitrogen fixation turns N2 into ammonia using bacteria, then nitrification turns that into nitrate, which plants take up through their roots and use to make amino acids and proteins.
(c)(i) NPP = GPP - R for each: 1100, 400, 200, 40.
(ii) Tropical rainforests have the highest GPP because it's warm and sunny there all year and there's a lot of rain, so plants can photosynthesize really well.
(d) My hypothesis is that removing sharks reduces diversity. I'd measure species diversity on reefs with and without sharks over 5 years and compare them. A limitation could be other environmental factors messing with the results.

(ii) Not sure of all three reasons, but one is that energy is lost as heat during respiration.
(iii) I think you'd need 5,000 kg of phytoplankton for the tuna, based on multiplying by 10% each time.

(ii) Ecological efficiency stays below 10% mainly because higher trophic levels are larger animals that need more energy just to maintain their bigger bodies, so less energy is available to be passed up further; the bigger and more complex the organism, the more energy it wastes just existing.
(iii) To support a 50 kg tuna, you'd need 50 x 10 x 10 = 5,000 kg of phytoplankton, counting the transfer from zooplankton to fish and from fish to tuna.

I'd measure fish counts on reefs with and without sharks over five years. A limitation is that reef fish are hard to count accurately.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) G1/S checkpoint: Growth factors bind cell surface receptors → activate signaling → stimulate synthesis of cyclin D. Cyclin D accumulates and binds CDK4/6 → active cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex phosphorylates Rb protein. Unphosphorylated Rb binds and sequesters E2F transcription factor → E2F inactive. Phosphorylated Rb (by cyclin D-CDK4/6) releases E2F. Free E2F activates transcription of S-phase genes (cyclin E, DNA polymerase components, etc.) → cell commits to S phase and DNA replication. (ii) Rb loss-of-function mutation: Rb cannot bind E2F → E2F is constitutively free → S-phase genes are always on → cell bypasses G1 checkpoint → continuous cell cycle progression without growth factor signals. Cancer consequence: cells proliferate uncontrollably; the G1 restriction point is the primary checkpoint preventing replication of cells with unrepaired DNA or inappropriate growth signals. Rb is a classic tumor suppressor. 1 pt for complete G1/S mechanism with all four named components; 1 pt for Rb mutation effect and cancer relevance.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe G1/S checkpoint molecular events; explain Rb mutation effect on cell cycle and cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: Growth factor → cyclin D synthesis → cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb → phospho-Rb releases E2F → E2F activates S-phase genes → S phase entry. Rb mutation: E2F permanently free → cells bypass G1 checkpoint → uncontrolled proliferation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Proto-oncogenes: (i) Normal function — encode proteins that promote cell growth, division, and survival in a regulated fashion: growth factors (PDGF), growth factor receptors (EGFR), intracellular signal transducers (RAS, Raf), transcription factors (Myc), cell cycle regulators. (ii) Mutation mechanism — gain-of-function mutations convert proto-oncogenes to oncogenes: point mutation (RAS G12V permanently active), gene amplification (Myc overexpressed), chromosomal translocation (BCR-ABL fusion), or promoter upregulation → constitutively active growth signaling. (iii) Dominant — one mutant allele is sufficient to drive abnormal proliferation (the gain-of-function allele dominates the wild-type). Tumor suppressor genes: (i) Normal function — encode proteins that restrain cell division, promote apoptosis, repair DNA, or maintain cell contact inhibition: Rb (G1 brake), p53 (DNA damage guardian), BRCA1/2 (DNA repair), APC (Wnt pathway brake). (ii) Mutation mechanism — loss-of-function mutations via point mutation, deletion, or epigenetic silencing eliminate the protein's brake function. (iii) Recessive (at cellular level / two-hit hypothesis) — both alleles must be inactivated to lose tumor suppressive function (one functional copy is usually sufficient). 1 pt per gene type with all three components correct.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Compare proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressors: normal function, how mutations drive cancer, dominant vs. recessive.
rubric.minimum_fix: Proto-oncogenes: promote growth in regulated manner; gain-of-function mutations (point mutation, amplification) → oncogenes → constitutive growth signals → dominant (one mutant allele sufficient). Tumor suppressors: brake cell division; loss-of-function mutations (both alleles, two-hit) → remove brakes → recessive at cellular level.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Intrinsic pathway: DNA damage or other intracellular stress → activates BH3-only pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins (Bim, Bid, Puma) → these inhibit anti-apoptotic proteins (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) → releases pro-apoptotic proteins Bax/Bak from inhibition → Bax/Bak oligomerize and permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane (MOMP) → cytochrome c released from mitochondrial intermembrane space into cytoplasm → cytochrome c + Apaf-1 + procaspase-9 → apoptosome complex → activates caspase-9 → activates executioner caspases (caspase-3, 6, 7) → cleave cellular substrates (DNA, cytoskeletal proteins, etc.) → apoptosis. (ii) Cancer cell evasion (any ONE mechanism): (1) Overexpression of Bcl-2 or Bcl-xL — blocks cytochrome c release; (2) Loss of Bax/Bak function via mutation; (3) p53 mutation or MDM2 amplification — p53 cannot activate Puma/Bim; (4) Activation of IAP (inhibitor of apoptosis proteins) that block caspase activation; (5) Elevated survival signaling (PI3K-Akt pathway phosphorylates Bad, keeping Bcl-2 active). 1 pt for correctly tracing intrinsic pathway with cytochrome c and caspases; 1 pt for one specific evasion mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the intrinsic apoptosis pathway; explain how cancer cells evade apoptosis.
rubric.minimum_fix: Intrinsic pathway: DNA damage → BH3-only proteins inhibit Bcl-2 → Bax/Bak permeabilize mitochondria → cytochrome c released → apoptosome → caspase-9 → executioner caspases → cell death. Cancer evasion example: Bcl-2 overexpression blocks cytochrome c release.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) p53 normal function: activated by DNA damage, oncogene activation, or hypoxia → induces transcription of p21 (CDK inhibitor, halts cell cycle) and pro-apoptotic genes → allows DNA repair or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable → prevents accumulation of mutations. E6 degrades p53 → cells with DNA damage cannot halt the cycle → mutations accumulate → cancer. (ii) E7 binds and functionally inactivates Rb → same as Rb loss-of-function: E2F is constitutively free → G1 checkpoint bypassed → cells replicate uncontrollably without growth factor signals. Mechanistically identical to Rb mutation in cancer cells. (iii) HPV vaccine is cancer prevention because: it prevents HPV infection before it occurs. Once HPV integrates into the host genome (occurring years to decades before cancer develops), the viral E6 and E7 genes become permanently expressed → p53 and Rb are continuously targeted. The vaccine cannot remove integrated viral DNA or restore p53/Rb function in already-infected cells. Cancer treatment would require eliminating already-transformed cells; prevention targets the infectious cause before transformation can begin. 1 pt for E6/p53 + E7/Rb mechanisms; 1 pt for prevention vs. treatment distinction with molecular reasoning.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain E6/p53, E7/Rb mechanisms; explain why HPV vaccine is cancer prevention not treatment.
rubric.minimum_fix: E6 degrades p53 → cells cannot arrest at DNA damage checkpoints → mutations accumulate → cancer. E7 inactivates Rb → same as Rb mutation → E2F free → bypass G1 checkpoint. Vaccine prevents HPV infection before viral integration; cannot remove integrated viral DNA or reverse p53/Rb inactivation in infected cells → prevention only, not treatment.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The cell cycle in eukaryotes is regulated by checkpoints that prevent cells from progressing to the next phase unless specific conditions are met.
    (i) Describe the molecular events at the G1/S checkpoint (restriction point). Include the roles of: cyclin D, CDK4/6, Rb protein, and E2F transcription factor.
    (ii) Explain how a mutation that permanently inactivates the Rb protein would affect cell cycle progression, and why such a mutation is commonly found in cancer cells.

(b) Compare the role of proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in regulating cell division. For each, explain: (i) the normal function; (ii) how mutations convert them into cancer-driving alleles; (iii) whether the cancer-causing mutation is typically dominant or recessive (at the cellular level), and why.

(c) Apoptosis (programmed cell death) is an important tumor-suppression mechanism.
    (i) Describe the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis. Include the roles of DNA damage signals, Bcl-2 family proteins, cytochrome c, and caspases.
    (ii) Explain how cancer cells commonly evade apoptosis, giving one specific molecular mechanism.

(d) Cervical cancer is strongly associated with infection by certain strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV). HPV encodes two oncoproteins, E6 and E7. E6 binds p53 and targets it for proteasomal degradation; E7 binds and inactivates the Rb protein.
    (i) Explain, using your knowledge of p53's normal function, why E6-mediated p53 degradation promotes cancer development.
    (ii) Explain why E7 inactivation of Rb produces a similar effect to a loss-of-function Rb mutation.
    (iii) A new HPV vaccine prevents infection by cancer-associated HPV strains. Explain why this vaccine is considered cancer prevention and not cancer treatment.
items.stimulus:
The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and mitotic phase (M). Key regulatory molecules:

• Cyclins: regulatory proteins whose concentration oscillates during the cell cycle
• CDKs (cyclin-dependent kinases): enzymes activated by cyclins; phosphorylate target proteins
• Rb (retinoblastoma protein): tumor suppressor; when unphosphorylated, binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors
• E2F: transcription factor that activates S-phase genes when released from Rb
• p53: tumor suppressor; activated by DNA damage; induces p21 (CDK inhibitor) and apoptosis
• Bcl-2 family: pro-apoptotic (Bax, Bak) and anti-apoptotic (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) proteins
• Caspases: proteases activated during apoptosis; cleave cellular components

Vaccine note: the HPV vaccine (Gardasil) targets HPV strains 16 and 18, which together cause ~70% of cervical cancers. It is a prophylactic vaccine that prevents HPV infection.

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) At the G1/S checkpoint, growth factor signaling stimulates synthesis of cyclin D, which binds and activates CDK4/6. The active cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex phosphorylates the Rb protein. Unphosphorylated Rb binds and sequesters E2F, keeping it inactive; once Rb is phosphorylated, it releases E2F, which activates transcription of S-phase genes, committing the cell to enter S phase.
(ii) If Rb is permanently inactivated by mutation, it can no longer bind and hold E2F, so E2F is constitutively free to activate S-phase genes regardless of growth factor signals. This allows the cell to bypass the G1 checkpoint and continuously proliferate without proper regulation, which is why loss-of-function Rb mutations are commonly found in cancer cells.
(b) Proto-oncogenes normally encode proteins that promote cell growth and division in a tightly regulated way, such as growth factors and growth factor receptors. Gain-of-function mutations convert these into oncogenes that drive constitutive, unregulated growth signaling; because only one mutant allele is needed, these mutations are dominant at the cellular level. Tumor suppressor genes normally encode proteins that restrain cell division, repair DNA, or trigger apoptosis, such as Rb and p53; loss-of-function mutations eliminate this braking function, but because one functional copy is usually sufficient for normal regulation, both alleles typically must be inactivated (the two-hit hypothesis) -- making these mutations recessive at the cellular level.
(c)(i) In the intrinsic apoptosis pathway, DNA damage activates pro-apoptotic BH3-only Bcl-2 family proteins, which inhibit the anti-apoptotic proteins Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, releasing Bax and Bak. Bax and Bak oligomerize and permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane, allowing cytochrome c to leak into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c combines with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9 to form the apoptosome, activating caspase-9, which activates executioner caspases like caspase-3 that cleave cellular components.
(ii) Cancer cells commonly evade apoptosis by overexpressing anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-2, which continues to inhibit Bax/Bak and prevent cytochrome c release even when DNA damage signals are present.
(d)(i) p53 is normally activated by DNA damage and induces p21 to halt the cell cycle, or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable. When E6 degrades p53, cells with damaged DNA can no longer pause the cycle or die, so mutations accumulate unchecked, driving cancer.
(ii) E7 binds and inactivates Rb, which has the same downstream consequence as a loss-of-function Rb mutation: E2F is freed to constitutively drive S-phase transcription, bypassing the G1 checkpoint.
(iii) The vaccine is cancer prevention rather than treatment because it prevents HPV infection before the virus can integrate into the host genome. Once integration occurs, E6 and E7 are permanently expressed, continuously degrading p53 and inactivating Rb -- the vaccine cannot remove already-integrated viral DNA or reverse these effects in already-infected cells.

(ii) If Rb doesn't work, E2F is always free, so the cell keeps dividing without stopping, which is why it's linked to cancer.
(b) Proto-oncogenes help cells grow normally, but mutations can turn them into oncogenes that cause too much growth, and this only needs one bad copy. Tumor suppressors normally stop cell division, but you usually need both copies messed up for cancer to happen.
(c)(i) DNA damage triggers proteins that let cytochrome c out of the mitochondria, which then activates caspases that cause the cell to die.
(ii) Cancer cells can evade apoptosis by making too much of the proteins that block it, like Bcl-2.
(d)(i) E6 gets rid of p53, so the cell can't stop and fix DNA damage, so mutations build up.
(ii) E7 does something similar to Rb mutations by messing with the same pathway.
(iii) The vaccine prevents infection so it stops the whole process before it starts, which is why it's prevention, not treatment.

(ii) If Rb stops working, the cell cycle would probably slow down because there's an error in one of the regulatory proteins.
