(a) Polygenic traits produce a continuous distribution because each gene independently causes a completely separate distinct category of phenotype, and when you add together enough of these separate categories from different genes, it starts to look continuous even though each individual gene is actually controlling a discrete trait class. For AaBbCc, since there are three heterozygous genes, the height would be exactly halfway between the shortest and tallest possible values, so 170 cm, with the tallest being AABBCC and shortest aabbcc.
(b) The heritability formula shows that height is about 90% environmental and 10% genetic, since a value of 0.90 close to 1 indicates how much of the variation comes from outside influences like diet and exercise rather than genes. Schizophrenia's lower value of 0.62 would then mean it is even more heavily influenced by environment than height is. MZ twins can differ because their genomes actually change slightly over time due to normal cell division, similar to how mutations build up with age.
(c) Phenotypic plasticity refers to genetic mutations that occur in response to environmental stress, allowing an organism's DNA to change and adapt within its own lifetime. The wheat genotype with the flattest line, Genotype Z, must be the most plastic because it can maintain the same yield despite environmental change, showing it adapted its genes to resist the environment. I would recommend Genotype Y for an unknown environment since its wide range shows it has the most genetic flexibility to handle whatever conditions arise.
(d) Phenotypic plasticity and genetic adaptation are essentially the same process happening on different timescales, both involving the organism's DNA sequence changing to match the environment. Genetic assimilation would be an example of a plastic trait like thorn production becoming permanently written into the DNA of individual plants that experienced heavy herbivory during their own lifetimes, which then gets passed to their offspring.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) PIC assembly: (1) A pioneer transcription factor or general factor recognizes the TATA box (core promoter element ~25 bp upstream of TSS) → TFIID (containing TBP, TATA-Binding Protein) binds the TATA box; TBP bends DNA. (2) TFIIA and TFIIB are recruited → TFIIB positions RNA pol II. (3) TFIIF enters with RNA pol II → stabilizes RNA pol II at promoter. (4) TFIIE and TFIIH join → TFIIH has helicase activity to unwind DNA at TSS (open complex formation) and kinase activity to phosphorylate the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA pol II → triggers elongation. Two GTFs to name: TFIID (TBP subunit recognizes TATA box), TFIIH (helicase opens DNA and CTD kinase activates polymerase). (ii) Enhancer mechanism: activator proteins bind the enhancer element via their DNA-binding domains. The activation domains of activators recruit coactivators and Mediator complex. The chromatin between enhancer and promoter loops around (enhancer-promoter looping, mediated by cohesin and CTCF proteins) → brings the activator-Mediator complex into contact with the PIC at the promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → stimulates transcription initiation rate. This looping explains action at a distance (10 kb away). 1 pt for PIC assembly with two GTFs and roles; 1 pt for enhancer-looping-Mediator mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe PIC assembly at eukaryotic promoter naming two GTFs; explain enhancer-Mediator mechanism.
rubric.minimum_fix: TFIID (TBP binds TATA box) and TFIIH (helicase opens DNA, CTD kinase activates RNA pol II) assemble PIC. Enhancer: activators bind → DNA loops (cohesin/CTCF) → enhancer contacts promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → increased transcription.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Euchromatin vs. heterochromatin at histone level: Euchromatin — histones are hyperacetylated (acetyl groups on lysine residues of H3 and H4 N-terminal tails) and have active histone methylation marks (H3K4me3 at promoters); chromatin is loose and accessible. Heterochromatin — histones are hypoacetylated (deacetylated), have repressive methylation marks (H3K9me3, H3K27me3); histone H1 (linker histone) compacts chromatin further; chromatin is condensed, DNA inaccessible. (ii) HAT/HDAC mechanism: HATs (histone acetyltransferases) add acetyl groups to histone lysine residues → neutralizes positive charge of lysine → reduces attraction between histones and negatively charged DNA → chromatin loosens (nucleosome-DNA interaction weakened) → DNA more accessible to transcription machinery → transcription increases. HDACs (histone deacetylases) remove acetyl groups → lysines revert to positive charge → stronger histone-DNA interactions → chromatin compacts → transcription decreases. (iii) Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor) effect: HDACs cannot remove acetyl groups → histones remain hyperacetylated → chromatin stays loose/open → global increase in transcription of many genes, including genes normally kept silenced. Genes under active repression via deacetylation would be de-repressed. Effect: widespread upregulation of gene expression; some previously silenced genes (tumor suppressors, differentiation genes) may be reactivated. This is why HDAC inhibitors are investigated as cancer therapies. 1 pt for euchromatin/heterochromatin marks with mechanism; 1 pt for correct HDAC inhibitor prediction with reasoning.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe euchromatin/heterochromatin histone modifications; HAT/HDAC mechanisms; predict HDAC inhibitor effect.
rubric.minimum_fix: Euchromatin: hyperacetylated histones (H3K4me3), loose chromatin. Heterochromatin: deacetylated histones (H3K9me3, H3K27me3), compact. HATs acetylate lysines → neutralize charge → looser chromatin → more transcription. HDACs remove acetyl → compact. HDAC inhibitor → all histones remain acetylated → global gene upregulation → silenced genes de-repressed.

accepted_variants: Mediator bridges activator to RNA pol II
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) DBD alone (expression = 1, baseline): the DNA-binding domain alone can bind the promoter but does NOT activate transcription — it shows that DNA binding is necessary but not sufficient for transcription activation. Simply recruiting a protein to the DNA does not stimulate RNA pol II. Transcriptional activation requires a separate activation domain. (ii) Activation domain results: activation domains differ in strength (AD3 > AD1 > AD2); the activation domain is the functional module responsible for stimulating transcription, independent of what DNA it is bound to (domain swap experiment works). Combining AD1 + AD3 gives superadditive (synergistic) activation (203 > 45+87 = 132) — demonstrates that multiple activation domains can work cooperatively (combinatorial activation), perhaps by recruiting different coactivators simultaneously. (iii) Mediator interaction of AD3: if AD3 physically contacts the Mediator complex, AD3 recruits Mediator to the promoter → Mediator acts as a bridge between activators and the general transcription machinery → Mediator interacts with RNA pol II CTD → stimulates assembly of the PIC or transition from initiation to productive elongation (CTD phosphorylation) → increased transcription. AD3's stronger activation could be because it makes particularly favorable contacts with Mediator subunits. 1 pt for correct interpretations of DBD alone + AD results; 1 pt for Mediator mechanism.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Interpret domain fusion experiment data; explain Mediator interaction mechanism.
rubric.minimum_fix: DBD alone: binding DNA insufficient for activation. ADs differ in strength; AD3 > AD1 > AD2. AD1+AD3 synergistic (203 > 132) = combinatorial activation. AD3-Mediator interaction: recruits Mediator to promoter → bridges activator to RNA pol II → stimulates PIC assembly or CTD phosphorylation → increased transcription.

accepted_variants: different TF combinations per cell type
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors: different cell types express different subsets of transcription factors; the combination of TFs present in a cell determines which genes are active. Gene A may require TF1 + TF2 + TF3 to be activated; Gene B requires TF1 + TF4. A neuron expresses TF1+TF2+TF3 (→ Gene A on, Gene B off); a muscle cell expresses TF1+TF4 (→ Gene A off, Gene B on). With as few as 10 different TFs, the combinatorial possibilities (2^10 = 1024 combinations) can specify hundreds of distinct cell identities. The same promoter is interpreted differently depending on which TFs are present → same genome, different expression profiles. (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states: once a cell commits to a lineage, its chromatin state (which regions are euchromatic vs. heterochromatic, DNA methylation at CpG islands, Polycomb/Trithorax marks on histones) is faithfully copied at each cell division. Maintenance methyltransferases (DNMT1) re-methylate hemimethylated DNA after replication. Histone modifications are self-perpetuating (Polycomb group proteins recognize their own mark → spread to newly deposited histones). This ensures that a liver cell's daughter cells remain liver cells and do not become neurons — the gene expression program is inherited epigenetically without changes in DNA sequence. 1 pt per mechanism correctly explained with cellular specificity logic.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain cell-type-specific expression via combinatorial TF control and epigenetic inheritance.
rubric.minimum_fix: Combinatorial TF control: different cell types have different TF combinations; each gene requires a specific TF combination; same genome interpreted differently per cell type. Epigenetic inheritance: chromatin marks (DNA methylation, H3K27me3) copied at each division; liver cell daughters remain liver cells; self-perpetuating chromatin states stabilize cell identity.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Eukaryotic gene expression requires the coordinated action of transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and chromatin remodeling.
    (i) Describe the sequence of events that leads to the assembly of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) at a eukaryotic promoter. Name TWO general transcription factors and their roles.
    (ii) Explain how an enhancer element located 10,000 base pairs upstream of a gene can stimulate transcription at the gene's promoter. Include the role of activator proteins and Mediator in your explanation.

(b) Chromatin structure regulates access to DNA. Using Figure 1 (which shows the same gene in euchromatin vs. heterochromatin states):
    (i) Describe the structural difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin at the level of histone modification.
    (ii) Explain how histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) have opposite effects on transcription. Include the mechanism by which acetylation opens chromatin.
    (iii) A researcher adds trichostatin A (an HDAC inhibitor) to cells. Predict and explain the effect on global gene expression.

(c) Experiment: The researcher fuses the DNA-binding domain of a transcription factor to different activation domains and measures target gene expression. Results are shown in Table 1. Interpret these results:
    (i) What does the DNA-binding domain alone demonstrate about gene activation?
    (ii) What do the activation domain results reveal about how transcription is activated?
    (iii) The researcher finds that activation domain 3 interacts physically with the Mediator complex. Explain how this interaction could lead to increased transcription.

(d) Explain how the following two mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression in a multicellular organism that has one genome but hundreds of distinct cell types:
    (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors
    (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states

• Heterochromatin: highly compact; 300nm fiber; DNA wound tightly; gene inaccessible → gene OFF

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) TFIID, containing TATA-binding protein, recognizes and binds the TATA box, bending the DNA, after which TFIIA and TFIIB position RNA polymerase II, TFIIF stabilizes it, and TFIIE and TFIIH join; TFIIH has helicase activity that unwinds the DNA at the transcription start site and kinase activity that phosphorylates the CTD of RNA polymerase II to trigger elongation. (ii) Activator proteins bound at the distant enhancer recruit the Mediator complex through their activation domains, and the DNA between the enhancer and promoter loops around, aided by cohesin and CTCF, bringing the activator-Mediator complex into contact with the pre-initiation complex at the promoter, where Mediator bridges the activators to RNA polymerase II and stimulates transcription initiation even though the enhancer is far away.
(b)(i) Euchromatin histones are hyperacetylated and carry active marks like H3K4me3, keeping chromatin loose and accessible, while heterochromatin histones are hypoacetylated and carry repressive marks like H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, keeping chromatin condensed and inaccessible. (ii) Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, neutralizing their positive charge and weakening the attraction to negatively charged DNA, loosening chromatin and increasing transcription, while histone deacetylases remove those acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge and compacting chromatin, decreasing transcription. (iii) Trichostatin A blocks HDACs, so histones remain hyperacetylated and chromatin stays open globally, leading to widespread upregulation of gene expression, including reactivation of genes that are normally silenced by deacetylation.
(c)(i) The DNA-binding domain alone shows that simply binding to the promoter is not sufficient to activate transcription; DNA binding is necessary but not enough on its own. (ii) The different activation domains show that transcriptional activation requires a distinct functional module beyond DNA binding, that these domains vary in strength (AD3 > AD1 > AD2), and that combining AD1 and AD3 gives a synergistic, more-than-additive increase in expression, showing that activation domains can work combinatorially. (iii) If AD3 physically contacts the Mediator complex, it likely recruits Mediator directly to the promoter, where Mediator bridges the activator to RNA polymerase II and stimulates assembly of the pre-initiation complex or CTD phosphorylation, increasing the rate of transcription initiation.
(d)(i) Combinatorial control means different cell types express different combinations of transcription factors, and each gene requires a specific combination to be switched on, so the same genome produces different expression patterns in different cell types depending on which factors are present. (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states, including DNA methylation patterns and histone modifications, is faithfully copied at each cell division by enzymes like DNMT1 and self-perpetuating Polycomb marks, ensuring that a cell's daughter cells retain the same gene expression program and identity, such as a liver cell always producing liver cell daughters.

(a) TFIID binds the TATA box to start assembling the machinery, and TFIIH helps unwind the DNA and get RNA polymerase II going. Enhancers work because activator proteins bind them and the DNA loops around so the activator can reach the promoter and help start transcription through Mediator.
(b) Euchromatin is more open and accessible, and heterochromatin is more closed off, and this has to do with how acetylated the histones are. HATs add acetyl groups that open chromatin, and HDACs remove them to close chromatin back up. If you block HDACs with something like trichostatin A, chromatin would probably stay open more and genes would likely get expressed more than usual.
(c) The DNA-binding domain by itself doesn't really do much to activate the gene since it just binds. The different activation domains have different strengths and some work better together. If AD3 touches Mediator, it's probably helping recruit the polymerase machinery somehow.
(d) Different cells have different transcription factors around, which lets the same genome make different proteins in different cell types. Cells also seem to remember their type after dividing because of some kind of chromatin marks getting passed down.
