(b) Euchromatin is open and heterochromatin is closed, and I think acetylation is involved in that somehow.
(c) Not sure what the DNA-binding domain results show. AD3 seems to be the strongest activation domain based on the numbers.
(d) Different cell types express different genes because of transcription factors.

(a) TFIID binds the TATA box, and TFIIH unwinds the DNA, but the actual signal to start transcription comes when RNA polymerase II itself recognizes the promoter sequence directly through its own DNA-binding domain, independent of the general transcription factors, which mainly help stabilize the complex rather than initiate it. Enhancers work by being transcribed themselves into a short RNA that diffuses through the nucleus and directly binds RNA polymerase II at the distant promoter, explaining action at a distance without any need for DNA looping.
(b) Heterochromatin is actually the more heavily acetylated form of chromatin, since all that extra positive charge from added acetyl groups causes the histones to clump together more tightly, forming the dense, compact structure. Euchromatin, by contrast, has fewer acetyl groups, leaving histones more neutral and loosely spaced apart. If HDACs were blocked by trichostatin A, chromatin would become more compact overall since acetyl groups would build up unchecked, and gene expression would decrease globally.
(c) The DNA-binding domain alone produces the highest expression on its own before any activation domains are added, since binding DNA directly is what recruits RNA polymerase II most efficiently; adding activation domains actually just gets in the way, which is why AD2 lowers expression compared to the baseline. The physical contact between AD3 and Mediator probably works by AD3 directly synthesizing a short burst of mRNA itself before the full polymerase complex arrives.
(d) Different cell types actually have slightly different genomes, since certain genes are physically deleted from the DNA in cells that don't need them, which is why a liver cell cannot express muscle genes even if you tried to activate them with transcription factors. Epigenetic marks are irrelevant to this because the genetic material itself has already been permanently altered during development.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Biogenesis: (1) miRNA gene transcribed by RNA polymerase II → primary miRNA (pri-miRNA) with hairpin stem-loop structure; (2) Drosha (nuclear RNase III enzyme) + cofactor DGCR8/Pasha recognizes and cleaves the hairpin → releases ~70-nucleotide precursor miRNA (pre-miRNA) hairpin; (3) Exportin-5 exports pre-miRNA to cytoplasm; (4) Dicer (cytoplasmic RNase III enzyme) cleaves the loop → generates ~22-bp miRNA duplex; (5) One strand of the duplex (guide strand) is loaded into Argonaute (AGO) protein → forms RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex); passenger strand is degraded. Two key enzymes: Drosha (nuclear processing) and Dicer (cytoplasmic duplex cleavage). (ii) Two silencing mechanisms: (A) mRNA cleavage: when miRNA has PERFECT or near-perfect complementarity to the target mRNA (common in plants; also in animal siRNA) → AGO's endonuclease (Slicer) activity cleaves the mRNA at the complementary site → mRNA degraded → no protein made. (B) Translational repression + mRNA destabilization: when miRNA has IMPERFECT complementarity (bulges, mismatches, typical for animal miRNAs) → RISC blocks ribosome translation without immediately cleaving → mRNA is also recruited to P-bodies (processing bodies) where it is deadenylated (poly-A tail removed), decapped, and degraded over time. 1 pt for biogenesis with Drosha/Dicer; 1 pt for both mechanisms with complementarity condition.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe miRNA biogenesis from gene to RISC; name Drosha and Dicer; explain two silencing mechanisms.
rubric.minimum_fix: miRNA gene → Drosha/DGCR8 → pre-miRNA → exported → Dicer → ~22nt duplex → guide strand loaded into AGO → RISC. Two mechanisms: (1) perfect complementarity → AGO Slicer cleavage; (2) imperfect complementarity → translational repression + deadenylation/decay in P-bodies.

accepted_variants: both mRNA degradation and translational repression
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Data interpretation: Wild-type 3'UTR + miRNA → 80% reduction in luciferase activity (100→20). Mutant 3'UTR + miRNA → no reduction (100→98; 2% variation is noise). Conclusion: the 3'UTR is required for miRNA-mediated silencing. The miRNA must bind to a complementary sequence in the 3'UTR to suppress translation or destabilize the mRNA. Removing the 3'UTR binding site (mutant) completely abolishes silencing → the 3'UTR sequence is the functional target of miRNA silencing. This demonstrates that miRNA silencing is sequence-specific (the miRNA must base-pair with the target 3'UTR) and that the 3'UTR is the cis-regulatory element mediating repression. (ii) mRNA decreases 30%, protein decreases 80% — discrepancy: miRNAs act by BOTH mRNA destabilization AND translational repression simultaneously. The 30% reduction in mRNA accounts for the mRNA degradation component. The additional 50% reduction in protein (beyond what the mRNA reduction would predict) reflects translational repression — ribosomes are blocked from efficiently translating the remaining mRNA. This demonstrates that translational repression is a major silencing mechanism independent of mRNA degradation. If silencing were purely through mRNA degradation, protein reduction would equal mRNA reduction. 1 pt for 3'UTR interpretation with mechanistic explanation; 1 pt for mRNA/protein discrepancy with translational repression.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Interpret reporter assay data; explain mRNA vs protein level discrepancy.
rubric.minimum_fix: 3'UTR required for silencing: miRNA binding site in 3'UTR necessary (mutant with no site shows no silencing); silencing is sequence-specific. Discrepancy: 30% mRNA reduction + 50% additional protein reduction = miRNA acts via both mRNA degradation AND translational repression simultaneously.

rubric.evidence_requirements: 5' cap (7-methylguanosine, m7G): Role in stability: the 5' cap protects the mRNA from 5'→3' exonuclease degradation; without the cap, 5'→3' exonucleases rapidly degrade the mRNA from the 5' end. Role in translation: the 5' cap is recognized by eIF4E (eukaryotic initiation factor 4E), which is part of the eIF4F cap-binding complex; eIF4E recruits the 43S ribosomal pre-initiation complex → ribosome scanning begins. Without 5' cap: mRNA is rapidly degraded; ribosomes cannot initiate translation efficiently → both stability and translation are severely impaired → essentially no protein produced. 3' poly-A tail (stretch of 100-250 adenine residues): Role in stability: poly-A tail + PABP (poly-A binding protein) protect the mRNA from 3'→5' exonuclease degradation. Deadenylation (removal of poly-A tail) is the first step in mRNA decay (deadenylation → decapping → degradation). Role in translation: PABP on the poly-A tail interacts with eIF4G at the 5' cap (circularization of mRNA) → promotes ribosome recycling and re-initiation → increases translation efficiency. Without poly-A tail: mRNA is rapidly degraded by exonucleases; translation efficiency reduced; reduced ribosome recycling. 1 pt per feature (5' cap + poly-A tail) with both stability AND translation roles + absence consequence.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain roles of 5' cap and poly-A tail in mRNA stability and translation; predict consequences of absence.
rubric.minimum_fix: 5' cap: protects from 5'→3' exonuclease; recognized by eIF4E → ribosome recruitment; absence = rapid decay + no translation. Poly-A tail: PABP protects from 3'→5' exonuclease; interacts with eIF4G for mRNA circularization and ribosome recycling; absence = rapid deadenylation decay + reduced translation efficiency.

accepted_variants: gene number does not equal proteome complexity
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Alternative splicing: the same pre-mRNA can be spliced in different ways in different cell types or conditions → different exon combinations are included in the mature mRNA → different polypeptide sequences (isoforms) are produced from the same gene. Mechanism — exon skipping: the spliceosome can be directed (by SR proteins and other splicing regulators) to skip over certain exons → they are spliced out with the introns rather than retained → shorter mRNA with different protein sequence. Example: the human DSCAM gene (neuronal adhesion); or tropomyosin gene in muscle vs. non-muscle cells — same pre-mRNA, different exons included → tissue-specific protein isoforms with different functional properties. Alternative splice sites: a splice donor (5' splice site) or acceptor (3' splice site) can be used at one of multiple positions → variable-length exons included. Intron retention: an intron is retained in the mature mRNA → produces a protein with the intron-encoded sequence, if it does not contain a premature stop codon. (ii) DSCAM and proteome complexity: Drosophila has ~13,600 genes total; DSCAM alone can produce >38,000 protein isoforms through combinatorial alternative splicing of multiple variable exon clusters (exon 4: 12 variants, exon 6: 48 variants, exon 9: 33 variants, exon 17: 2 variants → 12×48×33×2 = 38,016 combinations). This single gene produces more protein variants than the entire gene count of the organism. This reveals that gene number does not equal proteome complexity — alternative splicing dramatically amplifies the coding capacity of a genome beyond what gene counting alone would suggest. The "one gene, one polypeptide" model is an oversimplification. 1 pt for alternative splicing mechanism with example; 1 pt for DSCAM interpretation with numbers and conclusion.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain alternative splicing; describe one mechanism with example; interpret DSCAM numbers.
rubric.minimum_fix: Alternative splicing: different exon combinations → different protein isoforms from one gene. Exon skipping: spliceosome skips exons → shorter protein. Example: tropomyosin, DSCAM. DSCAM: 38,016 isoforms from 1 gene; Drosophila has 13,600 genes; more isoforms from one gene than total gene count; gene number ≠ proteome complexity.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.
    (i) Describe the biogenesis of a miRNA, beginning with the miRNA gene and ending with the functional RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex). Name the two key enzymes involved in miRNA processing.
    (ii) Explain the TWO molecular mechanisms by which miRNA-RISC can silence target mRNA expression. Specify the condition under which each mechanism predominates.

(b) Table 1 shows the results of an experiment in which a miRNA was introduced into cells expressing a reporter gene (luciferase). Cells were transfected with either a wild-type 3'UTR sequence or a mutant 3'UTR lacking the miRNA binding site.
    (i) Interpret the results. What do the data demonstrate about the role of the 3'UTR in miRNA-mediated silencing?
    (ii) The researcher observes that luciferase mRNA levels decrease by only 30% in wild-type cells, but luciferase protein decreases by 80%. Explain this discrepancy.

(c) Explain the role of the 5' cap (7-methylguanosine) and the 3' poly-A tail in mRNA stability and translation efficiency. For each, describe what happens to an mRNA that lacks that feature.

(d) Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA is a key mechanism for generating proteome diversity from a limited genome.
    (i) Explain how alternative splicing can generate multiple protein isoforms from a single gene. Describe one mechanism (exon skipping, alternative splice sites, or intron retention) and give a biological example.
    (ii) The gene DSCAM in Drosophila can produce more than 38,000 different protein isoforms through alternative splicing. Explain why this exceeds the number of genes in the entire Drosophila genome and what this reveals about the relationship between gene number and proteome complexity.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: miRNA reporter assay
Condition                        | Luciferase activity (relative units)
No miRNA, wild-type 3'UTR        |        100
miRNA added, wild-type 3'UTR     |         20
No miRNA, mutant 3'UTR           |        100
miRNA added, mutant 3'UTR        |         98

miRNA biogenesis summary:
• miRNA gene transcribed by RNA pol II → primary miRNA (pri-miRNA, hairpin structure)
• Drosha (nuclear RNase III) + DGCR8 → cleaves to ~70-nt pre-miRNA
• Exportin-5 → exported to cytoplasm
• Dicer (cytoplasmic RNase III) → cleaves pre-miRNA duplex → ~22-nt miRNA duplex
• One strand loaded into Argonaute (AGO) protein → RISC formed
• Guide strand targets complementary mRNA sequences (usually in 3'UTR)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) A miRNA gene is transcribed by RNA polymerase II into a hairpin-shaped pri-miRNA, which is cleaved in the nucleus by Drosha and its cofactor DGCR8 into a shorter pre-miRNA hairpin that is exported to the cytoplasm by Exportin-5; there, Dicer cleaves the loop to produce a roughly 22-nucleotide duplex, and the guide strand is loaded into an Argonaute protein to form the functional RISC complex. (ii) When the miRNA has near-perfect complementarity to its target, Argonaute's Slicer activity directly cleaves and degrades the mRNA, whereas when complementarity is imperfect, which is typical in animals, RISC instead blocks translation and recruits the mRNA to P-bodies for deadenylation and gradual decay.
(b)(i) Because silencing only occurs with the wild-type 3'UTR and disappears when the 3'UTR is mutated, the data show that the 3'UTR contains the sequence-specific binding site required for miRNA-mediated silencing, and without it the miRNA cannot act on the mRNA at all. (ii) The mRNA only decreases 30% while protein decreases 80%, showing that miRNA silencing works through both mRNA destabilization and translational repression simultaneously, so even the remaining mRNA is being translated less efficiently than normal, which explains the extra drop in protein beyond what mRNA loss alone would predict.
(c) The 5' cap protects the mRNA from 5'-to-3' exonuclease degradation and is recognized by eIF4E to recruit the ribosome for translation initiation, so an mRNA without a cap would be rapidly degraded and poorly translated. The poly-A tail, bound by PABP, protects the mRNA from 3'-to-5' exonuclease degradation and interacts with eIF4G to circularize the mRNA, promoting ribosome recycling and re-initiation, so an mRNA without a poly-A tail would be deadenylated and degraded quickly and translated less efficiently.
(d)(i) Alternative splicing allows the spliceosome to include different combinations of exons in the mature mRNA from the same pre-mRNA, for example through exon skipping directed by SR proteins, producing different protein isoforms in different tissues, as seen with the tropomyosin gene in muscle versus non-muscle cells. (ii) DSCAM can produce over 38,000 isoforms through combinatorial alternative splicing of its variable exon clusters, far more than the roughly 13,600 genes in the Drosophila genome, showing that a single gene's splicing capacity can exceed the entire gene count of the organism and that gene number alone does not determine proteome complexity.

(a) miRNA genes get transcribed and processed by Drosha and then Dicer to make a short double-stranded RNA, and one strand gets loaded into a protein complex called RISC that can silence mRNA. It can either cut the mRNA directly or just block it from being translated, depending on how well it matches.
(b) The 3'UTR seems to be important for the miRNA to work, since silencing doesn't happen when it's mutated. The mRNA and protein levels don't drop by the same amount, so the miRNA is probably doing more than just breaking down the mRNA.
(c) The 5' cap and poly-A tail both help protect the mRNA from being broken down and help it get translated. Without them the mRNA probably wouldn't last very long or make as much protein.
(d) Alternative splicing lets one gene make different proteins by including different exons. DSCAM makes way more isoforms than the number of genes in the fly, which shows splicing adds a lot of protein diversity.

(a) miRNAs are processed by Drosha and Dicer and end up in a complex that can silence genes.
(b) The 3'UTR is needed for the miRNA to work, since the mutant version didn't get silenced.
(c) Not sure exactly what the cap and poly-A tail do individually.
(d) Alternative splicing makes different proteins from one gene.

(a) A miRNA gene is transcribed and processed by Dicer in the nucleus first, forming the pre-miRNA, which is then exported to the cytoplasm where Drosha performs the final cleavage into the mature duplex before being loaded into RISC. Once in RISC, the miRNA mechanism always works by directly and completely degrading its target mRNA, regardless of how well the sequences match up, since that is the primary way animal miRNAs silence genes.
(b) The data show that the 3'UTR mutation actually made the miRNA bind even more tightly to the mRNA, which is why luciferase activity barely changed in the mutant condition, since a stronger, more efficient binding event produces a smaller measurable signal change. The difference between the 30% mRNA decrease and the 80% protein decrease suggests that the antibody used to measure luciferase protein was probably not very accurate, rather than reflecting any real biological mechanism.
(c) The 5' cap's main job is to mark the mRNA for destruction once translation is complete, so a capped mRNA is actually degraded faster than an uncapped one. The poly-A tail's primary role is to prevent the ribosome from binding at all until the appropriate signal arrives, so removing the poly-A tail would allow translation to begin immediately and increase protein output.
(d) Alternative splicing works by having the cell physically cut out and permanently delete unused exons from its genomic DNA in each cell type, which is why muscle cells and neurons have measurably different DNA content by adulthood. The DSCAM gene's 38,000 isoforms come from having that many nearly identical duplicate copies of the gene scattered across the genome rather than from splicing a single pre-mRNA in different ways.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Epigenetic inheritance: heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in the DNA sequence. Marks are on the chromatin (DNA or histones) rather than in the base sequence itself. Unlike mutations (sequence changes), epigenetic marks can in principle be reversed. They are passed from parent cell to daughter cells during mitosis; some cross generational boundaries. (ii) Two major classes + silencing marks: DNA methylation — addition of methyl group to cytosine at CpG dinucleotides, catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). Mark associated with silencing: methylated CpG (5-methylcytosine, 5mC) at promoter CpG islands → gene repression. Histone modification — covalent modifications to N-terminal histone tails (methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination). Mark associated with silencing: H3K9me3 (trimethylation of lysine 9 on histone H3) or H3K27me3 (added by Polycomb group proteins). (iii) Chain of events — DNA methylation → transcriptional repression: CpG islands are methylated (5mC) → methyl-binding proteins (MBDs, e.g., MeCP2) recognize and bind methylated CpG → MeCP2 recruits HDAC complexes → histone deacetylation → chromatin compaction → transcription factor binding inhibited OR DNA methylation directly blocks transcription factor binding (if TF binding site overlaps with CpG) → RNA pol II cannot be recruited → gene silenced. 1 pt for definition + two marks; 1 pt for methylation → repression chain.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Define epigenetic inheritance; describe DNA methylation and histone modification silencing marks; explain CpG → repression chain.
rubric.minimum_fix: Epigenetic: heritable gene expression changes without DNA sequence change. DNA methylation at CpG islands (5mC) silences; H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 histone marks silence. Chain: 5mC → MeCP2 binds → recruits HDACs → histone deacetylation → chromatin compact → transcription blocked.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Igf2/H19 imprinting via ICR: Maternal chromosome: ICR is unmethylated → CTCF insulator protein binds the ICR → CTCF acts as a chromatin insulator/loop domain boundary → blocks the downstream enhancers from activating the upstream Igf2 gene → Igf2 is SILENCED on maternal chromosome. The enhancers instead activate H19 → H19 is expressed maternally. Paternal chromosome: ICR is methylated → CTCF cannot bind → insulator function abolished → downstream enhancers freely loop to and activate Igf2 → Igf2 is EXPRESSED paternally. H19 is also silenced on paternal chromosome (methylation spreads). Result: Igf2 is only expressed from the paternal copy (paternal imprinting). (ii) Imprinting disorder: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS): caused by loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13 (typically deletion of paternal 15q11-q13 OR maternal uniparental disomy where both copies of 15 come from mother → only maternal-imprinted [silenced] copies present → critical paternal genes not expressed). Features: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability. The genes affected include SNRPN (paternally expressed). OR: Angelman syndrome: loss of maternally expressed UBE3A in the same region. (iii) Parental conflict hypothesis (David Haig): in species where offspring of one female can have different fathers, each parent's genes are "in conflict." Paternal genes maximize growth of current offspring (extracts maximum resources from mother) → paternal alleles promote growth factors (Igf2). Maternal genes favor restraint (protect mother's ability to have future offspring with other mates) → maternal alleles suppress growth or act via growth inhibitors. This predicts that paternally imprinted genes (maternally expressed) tend to limit growth; maternally imprinted genes (paternally expressed) tend to promote growth — matches Igf2 (paternal, growth promoter) and H19 (maternal, growth inhibitor). 1 pt for ICR mechanism; 1 pt for disorder or parental conflict.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain ICR/Igf2 imprinting mechanism; describe imprinting disorder; explain parental conflict hypothesis.
rubric.minimum_fix: ICR unmethylated (maternal): CTCF binds → blocks Igf2 enhancer → Igf2 OFF, H19 ON. ICR methylated (paternal): CTCF absent → enhancer activates Igf2 → Igf2 ON. PWS: paternal 15q11 lost → paternal-expressed genes absent. Parental conflict: paternal alleles promote growth (Igf2); maternal alleles restrain (H19).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Trend: at age 3, MZ twins have very high epigenetic similarity (r = 0.94–0.98, nearly identical methylation patterns). At age 50, similarity has decreased substantially (r = 0.42–0.79). The twins' epigenomes diverge progressively with age — epigenetic differences accumulate over a lifetime despite identical DNA sequences. This demonstrates that epigenetic marks are influenced by environmental and stochastic factors, not solely genotype. (ii) Two mechanisms for divergence: (1) Different environmental exposures: different diets, smoking, stress, exercise, toxin exposure → different signals reaching cells → different DNMT or TET enzyme activity → different methylation patterns acquired at specific CpG sites. (2) Stochastic (random) epigenetic errors during DNA replication: during each cell division, maintenance methyltransferase (DNMT1) copies methylation patterns onto daughter strands, but errors occur at low frequency (~1/1000 CpGs per division); over millions of cell divisions across 50 years, these errors accumulate differently in each twin → diverging epigenomes. (iii) Transgenerational transmission: epigenetic marks are largely RESET (erased) during gametogenesis and early embryogenesis (global demethylation waves). Most methylation is cleared in primordial germ cells and re-established based on sex. For most loci: no, these somatic epigenetic differences would NOT be inherited by children. However, imprinted regions and certain transposable element-associated loci escape demethylation and can be transmitted. Examples of true transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals remain controversial but include agouti mouse coat color via methylation of an IAP element. 1 pt for data trend interpretation; 1 pt for two mechanisms OR transgenerational explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Interpret MZ twin methylation divergence data; propose mechanisms; explain transgenerational transmission.
rubric.minimum_fix: Trend: high similarity at age 3 (r ~0.96), lower at age 50 (r ~0.59 average) — epigenomes diverge with age. Mechanisms: (1) different environmental exposures; (2) stochastic replication errors in DNMT1 copying. Transgenerational: most epigenetic marks erased during gametogenesis/early embryo (demethylation); most somatic marks not inherited; exceptions: imprinted regions, some transposons.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Environmental example: Dutch Hunger Winter (1944-45): Dutch women pregnant during Nazi food blockade (severe caloric restriction ~500 cal/day for months) gave birth to children who, as adults, had altered methylation at the IGF2 imprinting control region, higher rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, schizophrenia, and type 2 diabetes compared to siblings conceived before or after the famine. The prenatal nutrient restriction altered DNMT activity during critical developmental windows → different methylation patterns established at key metabolic loci → these patterns influenced lifelong gene expression and metabolism. Other acceptable examples: maternal stress → glucocorticoid receptor methylation changes in offspring; cigarette smoke → specific methylation changes. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance mechanism: For epigenetic marks to be inherited across generations, they must escape the two waves of epigenetic reprogramming: (1) in the primordial germ cells (PGC reprogramming — demethylation of most of the genome); (2) after fertilization (post-fertilization demethylation and re-methylation). A mark that survives both waves in the germline will be transmitted to offspring. Mechanisms of escape: (A) Certain transposable elements (like IAP retrotransposons in mice) retain methylation through reprogramming; (B) Imprinted loci have protected methylation marks; (C) Histone modifications (H3K9me3, H3K27me3) on some loci are reestablished post-fertilization using residual histone information. Consequence: offspring of stressed/nutrition-deprived parents can inherit altered metabolic programming without any DNA sequence change. 1 pt for specific environmental example with mechanism; 1 pt for transgenerational mechanism with at least one escape mechanism named.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe one environmental epigenetic change; explain transgenerational epigenetic inheritance mechanism.
rubric.minimum_fix: Dutch Hunger Winter: prenatal famine → altered IGF2 methylation in offspring → increased disease risk in adulthood (obesity, CVD, schizophrenia). Transgenerational inheritance: marks must escape two demethylation waves (PGC reprogramming + post-fertilization). Escape mechanisms: IAP transposons retain methylation; imprinted loci protected; histone marks re-established.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Epigenetic modifications alter gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
    (i) Define epigenetic inheritance and explain how it differs from sequence-based genetic inheritance.
    (ii) Describe the two major classes of epigenetic modification (DNA methylation and histone modification), identifying a specific mark associated with gene silencing for each.
    (iii) Explain how DNA methylation at CpG island promoters causes gene silencing at the molecular level — describe the chain of events from methyl-CpG to transcriptional repression.

(b) Genomic imprinting results in the expression of only one parental allele for certain genes.
    (i) Using the Igf2/H19 imprinting locus as an example, explain how differential DNA methylation of the imprinting control region (ICR) leads to monoallelic expression.
    (ii) Explain why imprinting defects (such as loss of imprinting) can cause developmental disorders. Use Prader-Willi syndrome or Angelman syndrome as a specific example.
    (iii) Explain why most imprinted genes are involved in fetal growth and nutrient acquisition, citing the parental conflict hypothesis.

(c) Identical twins (MZ twins) are born with nearly identical genomes, yet they can develop different diseases as they age. Table 1 shows methylation data at four CpG sites in young (age 3) vs. older (age 50) MZ twin pairs.
    (i) Interpret the data: what trend do you observe in epigenetic similarity with age?
    (ii) Propose TWO mechanisms that could explain why MZ twins's epigenomes diverge over time.
    (iii) Explain whether these epigenetic differences would be passed to the twins' children.

(d) Environmental factors can alter epigenetic marks and potentially affect offspring. Describe ONE specific example of environmentally induced epigenetic change and its consequences, and explain the concept of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance — the mechanism by which epigenetic marks acquired in one generation can affect the next.
items.stimulus:
Table 1: Epigenome similarity (methylation correlation, r) in MZ twin pairs
CpG site | Similarity (r) at age 3 | Similarity (r) at age 50
    1    |         0.97            |          0.54
    2    |         0.95            |          0.61
    3    |         0.98            |          0.79
    4    |         0.94            |          0.42

Note: r = 1.0 means twins have identical methylation; r = 0 means no correlation.

Igf2/H19 locus:
• Maternal chromosome: ICR is UNMETHYLATED → CTCF insulator protein binds → blocks Igf2 enhancer from reaching Igf2 gene → Igf2 OFF; H19 is expressed
• Paternal chromosome: ICR is METHYLATED → CTCF cannot bind → Igf2 enhancer freely activates Igf2 → Igf2 ON; H19 is silenced by methylation

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) Epigenetic inheritance refers to heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve any change in the DNA sequence itself, unlike mutations, and these marks are passed from parent cells to daughter cells during mitosis. (ii) DNA methylation adds methyl groups to cytosines at CpG islands, with 5-methylcytosine at promoters associated with silencing, while histone modification adds marks like H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 to histone tails, which are also associated with repression. (iii) Methylated CpG islands are bound by methyl-binding proteins like MeCP2, which recruit HDAC complexes that deacetylate histones, compacting chromatin and blocking transcription factor binding, so RNA polymerase cannot be recruited and the gene is silenced.
(b)(i) On the maternal chromosome the ICR is unmethylated, so CTCF binds it and acts as an insulator that blocks the downstream enhancer from reaching Igf2, silencing Igf2 and allowing H19 to be expressed instead; on the paternal chromosome the ICR is methylated, so CTCF cannot bind, the insulator function is lost, and the enhancer freely activates Igf2. (ii) Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternally expressed genes in the 15q11-q13 region, whether through deletion or maternal uniparental disomy, causing hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and intellectual disability because the paternal-specific genes are never expressed. (iii) The parental conflict hypothesis explains this pattern because paternal alleles favor maximizing growth and resource extraction from the mother to benefit the current offspring, as with Igf2, while maternal alleles favor restraining growth to conserve the mother's resources for future offspring, as with H19.
(c)(i) Epigenetic similarity between MZ twins is very high at age 3 but decreases substantially by age 50, showing that the twins' epigenomes diverge progressively over their lifetimes despite identical DNA. (ii) This divergence likely results from different environmental exposures such as diet, smoking, or stress altering methylation patterns differently in each twin, and from stochastic replication errors accumulating differently over millions of cell divisions across decades. (iii) Most of these somatic epigenetic differences would not be passed to children because epigenetic marks are largely erased during gametogenesis and early embryogenesis through global demethylation waves, though some imprinted regions and certain transposon-associated loci can escape this reprogramming.
(d) The Dutch Hunger Winter is a well-documented example, where prenatal exposure to severe famine altered methylation at the IGF2 imprinting control region in the children, and as adults these individuals showed higher rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders. For an epigenetic mark to be transmitted to the next generation it must survive two waves of reprogramming, first in the primordial germ cells and again after fertilization, and marks that escape these waves, such as those on certain retrotransposons or imprinted loci, can be passed on and influence offspring phenotypes without any change to the DNA sequence.

(a) Epigenetic inheritance is when gene expression changes without the DNA sequence changing. It involves things like DNA methylation and histone modifications, and these marks tend to silence genes when they build up at a promoter, partly by making the chromatin more compact.
(b) The Igf2/H19 region has a control region that's methylated differently depending on which parent it came from, and that determines whether Igf2 or H19 gets expressed. When imprinting goes wrong, disorders like Prader-Willi syndrome can happen. There's also an idea that paternal genes want more growth and maternal genes want less, which is why it matters which parent's copy stays active.
(c) MZ twins start out really similar epigenetically but drift apart as they get older, probably due to environment and just random changes over time. I don't think those changes would necessarily get passed on to their kids since a lot of that stuff gets reset during reproduction.
(d) The Dutch Hunger Winter is an example where a mother's starvation affected her baby's health later in life through epigenetic changes. For these changes to be inherited by the next generation, they'd have to somehow survive the resetting that normally happens in the germ cells.

(a) Epigenetic changes affect gene expression without changing the DNA sequence, like DNA methylation.
(b) I know the Igf2/H19 locus is imprinted, but I don't remember the specific ICR mechanism.
(c) MZ twins seem to become less similar epigenetically over time.
(d) Not sure of a specific example.

(a) Epigenetic inheritance refers to small mutations in the DNA sequence that occur gradually and get passed down through generations, distinguishing it from regular genetic inheritance which involves the original, unmutated sequence. DNA methylation and histone acetylation are the two major classes, and both marks, when added to a promoter, actually increase gene expression by making the region more chemically reactive to RNA polymerase.
(b) On the maternal chromosome, the ICR is methylated, which activates CTCF binding and allows CTCF to directly recruit the enhancer to switch on Igf2, meaning Igf2 is actually expressed from the maternal copy. Prader-Willi syndrome results from an extra copy of the maternal chromosome 15 material, which overactivates growth genes and causes the associated features. The parental conflict hypothesis suggests that maternal genes want to maximize the current offspring's growth since the mother directly benefits from a larger, healthier baby right away.
(c) MZ twins' epigenomes become more similar with age as their shared environment and lifestyle gradually synchronize their gene expression patterns over the decades. Any differences that do exist are almost entirely due to one twin simply having a slightly different DNA sequence from birth. These shared epigenetic patterns, once synchronized, would very likely be passed on efficiently to both of their children.
(d) The Dutch Hunger Winter demonstrated that prenatal starvation had no lasting effect once normal food access resumed, since the body's epigenome fully resets within a few years after any environmental stressor ends. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance mainly happens through direct physical contact between a mother and her children after birth, rather than through anything transmitted via the germline.

accepted_variants: beak size data sympatric vs allopatric
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Allopatric speciation: speciation driven by geographic isolation. Population split by a physical barrier → separated populations cannot interbreed → genetic drift, mutation, and differential natural selection act independently on each population → populations diverge genetically → after sufficient time, populations are reproductively isolated even if geographic barrier is removed. Applied to Galápagos finches: (1) Original founder population from South America colonized one island; (2) Some individuals dispersed (over-water colonization) to other islands → geographic isolation on different islands; (3) Different island environments (food types, competitors, predators) applied different natural selection pressures → beaks and body size diverged on each island; (4) Eventually, sufficient genetic divergence → speciation; (5) Secondary colonization events brought different species back to same island (sympatry) → by this time, reproductive isolation had evolved → no interbreeding. This radiation produced multiple ecological niches occupied by different finch species (adaptive radiation). (ii) Character displacement: when two species co-occur (sympatry), competition for the same resource (e.g., medium seeds) intensifies. Natural selection favors individuals in each species that specialize on DIFFERENT resources → divergent selection → beak sizes diverge. Data: G. fortis and G. fuliginosa have almost identical beak depths when alone (11.0 vs. 10.5 mm) but diverge dramatically when co-occurring (13.5 vs. 8.0 mm). This competitive release of niche differentiation is character displacement. 1 pt for allopatric speciation sequence applied to finches; 1 pt for character displacement with data.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain allopatric speciation and Galápagos finch adaptive radiation; explain character displacement.
rubric.minimum_fix: Allopatric speciation: geographic isolation → independent evolution → reproductive isolation. Finches: South American ancestor → colonized different islands → different selection pressures → beak divergence → new species → secondary sympatry. Character displacement: sympatric species diverge in beak size due to competition; data shows beak depths more different when together (13.5 vs 8.0 mm) than when apart (11.0 vs 10.5 mm).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Frogs breeding at different times: PREZYGOTIC — temporal isolation. Gametes of the two species never meet because they breed at different times. (ii) Horse × donkey → sterile mule: POSTZYGOTIC — hybrid sterility. The species can mate and produce viable offspring but the offspring (mule) are sterile (2n = 63, cannot complete meiosis due to unequal chromosome number → no viable gametes). (iii) Meadowlarks with species-specific songs: PREZYGOTIC — behavioral (ethological) isolation. Female only responds to conspecific male song → mating behavior does not occur between species → gametes never meet. (iv) Plants with different pollinators: PREZYGOTIC — mechanical isolation (some texts: ecological isolation). If pollinators are the vector for pollen transfer and each species uses a different pollinator, pollen cannot be transferred between species → no fertilization possible. Alternatively classified as ecological isolation if the mechanism is broader than just flower morphology. Accept either classification with justification. Award 0.5 pt per correct classification and mechanism name, max 2 pts.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify four isolation mechanisms as prezygotic or postzygotic with specific names.
rubric.minimum_fix: (i) Temporal isolation (prezygotic). (ii) Hybrid sterility (postzygotic). (iii) Behavioral/ethological isolation (prezygotic). (iv) Mechanical or ecological isolation (prezygotic).

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Allopolyploidy: two different species hybridize → hybrid inherits one genome set from each parent species → hybrid is typically sterile (chromosomes cannot pair at meiosis because homologs are absent). If chromosome doubling occurs (spontaneously, or induced by colchicine) → allopolyploid with complete sets from both parents → now has homologs for ALL chromosomes → can complete meiosis and produce viable gametes. Immediate reproductive isolation: the new allopolyploid (4n) can only mate with itself (autogamy) or other same-4n individuals; cannot successfully mate with either parent species (different ploidy → aneuploid offspring) → instantly reproductively isolated from both parent species → new species in one generation. No geographic isolation required → sympatric speciation. (ii) More common in plants: plants can self-fertilize (autogamy) → polyploid individual can reproduce without finding a mate of the same ploidy; many plants reproduce asexually or vegetatively → polyploid can persist even if rare; plants more tolerant of aneuploidy; animals have chromosome dosage-sensitive sex determination systems that fail in polyploids. (iii) Bread wheat hexaploidy: T. urartu (AA, 2n=14) × Aegilops speltoides (BB, 2n=14) → hybrid (AB, sterile) → chromosome doubling → T. turgidum emmer wheat (AABBDD, 4n=28) → wait: AABB emmer (4n=28) × Aegilops tauschii (DD, 2n=14) → hybrid (ABD, sterile) → chromosome doubling → T. aestivum bread wheat (AABBDD, 6n=42). Three ancestral diploid genomes combined; each set of 7 chromosomes can pair → bread wheat is fertile and productive. 1 pt for allopolyploidy + immediate isolation; 1 pt for plant-animal difference + bread wheat.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain polyploid sympatric speciation; explain plant-animal difference; explain bread wheat hexaploidy.
rubric.minimum_fix: Allopolyploidy: hybrid of two species → sterile (no homologs) → chromosome doubling → homologs present → fertile polyploid; cannot mate with parental diploids (different ploidy) → immediate reproductive isolation without geographic separation. Plants: can self-fertilize, vegetative propagation, tolerant of ploidy changes. Bread wheat: T. urartu (AA) × Aegilops (BB) → AABB emmer × Aegilops (DD) → AABBDD hexaploid (6n=42).

rubric.evidence_requirements: Limitation 1: The BSC cannot be applied to asexual (clonal) organisms or fossil species. Bacteria reproduce asexually and undergo horizontal gene transfer — the concept of interbreeding populations does not apply. Fossils cannot be observed to interbreed. Best alternative: Phylogenetic (evolutionary) species concept — defines a species as the smallest monophyletic group diagnosable by shared derived characters (synapomorphies). Can be applied to asexual organisms and fossils using molecular or morphological data; based on evolutionary history rather than mating. Limitation 2: The BSC cannot handle situations where two populations can occasionally interbreed (hybridize) but remain distinct. Many plant species (e.g., oaks) hybridize frequently yet remain recognizable species. Also, ring species (like Ensatina salamanders in California) produce chains where adjacent populations interbreed but terminal populations do not. Best alternative: Ecological species concept — defines a species as a lineage occupying a distinct ecological niche (adaptive zone). Species remain distinct because they occupy different ecological roles; limited hybridization does not dissolve species boundaries as long as they maintain distinct ecological niches. This works for hybridizing plant species that occupy different habitats. 1 pt per limitation + matching alternative concept with reasoning.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe two BSC limitations and best alternative concepts.
rubric.minimum_fix: Limitation 1: does not apply to asexual organisms (bacteria) or fossils. Alternative: Phylogenetic species concept — uses synapomorphies and monophyly; applies to any organism regardless of reproduction. Limitation 2: cannot handle occasional hybridization between distinct species. Alternative: Ecological species concept — species = distinct ecological niche; hybridization allowed as long as ecological roles remain separate.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The Galápagos Islands are home to 14 species of Darwin's finches, all descended from a common South American ancestor that colonized the islands about 2–3 million years ago.
    (i) Explain allopatric speciation and apply it to the adaptive radiation of Galápagos finches. Describe the sequence of events from the original colonization to the presence of multiple species on the same island.
    (ii) Explain the role of natural selection in shaping beak morphology across finch species. Use the concept of character displacement to explain why sympatric species on the same island tend to have more different beak sizes than allopatric populations of the same species on different islands.

(b) Reproductive isolating mechanisms prevent gene flow between species. Classify each of the following as prezygotic or postzygotic and give the specific mechanism name:
    (i) Two species of frogs breed in the same pond but one breeds in early spring and one in late spring.
    (ii) A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, but mules are sterile.
    (iii) Eastern and western meadowlarks look nearly identical but have different songs — females only respond to their own species' song.
    (iv) Two species of plants have flowers adapted to different pollinators (bumblebees vs. hummingbirds).

(c) Sympatric speciation can occur without geographic isolation.
    (i) Explain how polyploidy can cause sympatric speciation in plants. Give a specific type (allopolyploidy or autopolyploidy) and describe how it creates immediate reproductive isolation.
    (ii) Explain why polyploid speciation is much more common in plants than in animals.
    (iii) Modern bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a hexaploid (6n = 42). Explain how it likely arose from hybridization events between ancestral diploid (2n=14) species.

(d) The biological species concept (BSC) defines species as groups of actually or potentially interbreeding populations that are reproductively isolated from other groups. Describe TWO limitations of the BSC and explain which alternative species concept (morphological, phylogenetic, or ecological) best addresses each limitation.
items.stimulus:
Darwin's finch diversity on the Galápagos:
• Ground finches (Geospiza): thick beaks, crush seeds of varying hardness
• Tree finches (Camarhynchus): grip-and-pry beaks, eat insects in woody vegetation
• Warbler finch (Certhidea): slender beak, glean tiny insects
• Woodpecker finch (Camarhynchus pallidus): uses cactus spine as tool to extract insects

Character displacement data:
Beak depth (mm) of Geospiza species:
Island type              | G. fortis | G. fuliginosa
Allopatric (each alone)  |  11.0 mm  |   10.5 mm
Sympatric (together)     |  13.5 mm  |    8.0 mm

Polyploidy examples:
• Allopolyploidy: two different species hybridize → combine both genome sets → new species
• Bread wheat = T. urartu (AA, 2n=14) × Aegilops speltoides (BB, 2n=14) → T. turgidum (AABB, 4n=28, emmer wheat) × Aegilops tauschii (DD, 2n=14) → T. aestivum (AABBDD, 6n=42, bread wheat)

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) Allopatric speciation occurs when a population is split by a geographic barrier so that gene flow stops, allowing genetic drift, mutation, and different selection pressures to act independently until the separated populations become reproductively isolated. For Darwin's finches, an ancestral South American population colonized one island, some individuals dispersed to other islands, different island environments imposed different selection pressures on beak size and shape, and eventually enough divergence accumulated that secondary contact between islands did not lead to interbreeding. (ii) Character displacement shows that when two Geospiza species live together, competition for the same seed resources drives their beak sizes to diverge as each specializes on a different food source, which matches the data showing beak depths of 13.5 mm and 8.0 mm when sympatric versus only 11.0 mm and 10.5 mm when allopatric.
(b)(i) Frogs breeding at different times shows temporal isolation, a prezygotic mechanism. (ii) A sterile mule from a horse-donkey cross shows hybrid sterility, a postzygotic mechanism. (iii) Meadowlarks responding only to their own species' song shows behavioral isolation, a prezygotic mechanism. (iv) Plants pollinated by different animals show mechanical or ecological isolation, a prezygotic mechanism.
(c)(i) Allopolyploidy occurs when two different species hybridize and the hybrid's chromosomes double, giving it a complete matching set from each parent species so it can pair properly at meiosis and produce viable gametes; because it can no longer successfully mate with either diploid parent species due to the ploidy mismatch, it is immediately reproductively isolated without any geographic separation, making this sympatric speciation. (ii) Polyploid speciation is more common in plants because many plants can self-fertilize or reproduce vegetatively, letting a single polyploid individual persist and reproduce without needing another polyploid mate, and plants tolerate changes in chromosome number better than animals do. (iii) Bread wheat likely arose when T. urartu hybridized with Aegilops speltoides and doubled to form tetraploid emmer wheat, which then hybridized with Aegilops tauschii and doubled again to form the hexaploid AABBDD genome of modern bread wheat.
(d) One limitation of the biological species concept is that it cannot be applied to asexual organisms or fossils, since there is no interbreeding to observe, and the phylogenetic species concept, which defines species by shared derived characters and monophyly, works better there because it does not depend on reproduction. Another limitation is that it cannot handle species that occasionally hybridize but remain ecologically distinct, such as some oak species, and the ecological species concept, which defines a species by its distinct ecological niche, better accounts for species that stay separate because they occupy different adaptive zones even with some gene flow.

(a) Allopatric speciation happens when populations get separated geographically and evolve independently until they can't interbreed anymore. The finches spread to different islands and developed different beak shapes because of different food sources, eventually becoming separate species. Character displacement is when species that live together end up with more different traits than when they live apart, which the beak data seems to show.
(b) Frogs breeding at different times is prezygotic. The mule being sterile is postzygotic. Meadowlarks with different songs is prezygotic. Plants with different pollinators is prezygotic too.
(c) Polyploidy can create a new species right away because the new individual can't breed with the original species anymore. This happens more in plants because they can self-pollinate. Bread wheat came from multiple hybridization events between different wild wheat relatives that combined their chromosomes.
(d) The biological species concept doesn't work well for things that reproduce asexually, so you'd need a different definition based on shared traits instead. It also doesn't work great when species hybridize sometimes but still act like separate species, so you might use something based on ecological niche instead.

(a) Allopatric speciation happens due to geographic separation, and the finches evolved different beaks on different islands.
(b) Frogs breeding at different times is prezygotic. Mule sterility is postzygotic. Not sure about the meadowlark and plant examples.
(c) Polyploidy involves extra copies of chromosomes leading to a new species.
(d) Not sure of specific limitations of the biological species concept.

(a) Allopatric speciation actually requires the two populations to remain in contact so that competition directly forces them to specialize on different resources, which is how the Galapagos finches ended up with different beaks even while living on the same islands the whole time. Character displacement shows that species become more similar to each other over time as they adapt to share the same environment efficiently, which is why sympatric beak measurements would be expected to converge rather than diverge.
(b) Frogs breeding at different times is actually postzygotic isolation, since the timing difference occurs after the frogs have already developed as separate species. A sterile mule demonstrates prezygotic isolation because the horse and donkey gametes must be incompatible at the moment of fertilization for the offspring to turn out sterile. Meadowlark song differences and plant-pollinator differences would both be classified as postzygotic since they involve developmental differences that show up later in the organism's life.
(c) Autopolyploidy from hybridizing two different species is the main route to instant reproductive isolation, since combining two different species' chromosomes directly doubles the ploidy without needing any actual chromosome doubling event to occur. Polyploidy is more common in plants mainly because plant cells have rigid cell walls that physically make it easier to fit extra chromosomes inside the nucleus. Bread wheat's hexaploid genome came from one single hybridization event between two wild grasses that happened to each contribute three complete genomes at once.
(d) The biological species concept struggles mainly with large animals like elephants, since their long generation times make it hard to observe interbreeding directly, so a phylogenetic concept based on body size differences works better for them. It also has trouble with species that live in exactly the same habitat, which is best resolved using the morphological species concept based on genetic sequence identity rather than physical appearance.

accepted_variants: cladogram B C D E nested
B sister to C D E
rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Synapomorphy: a shared derived character state that evolved in the common ancestor of a clade and is present in all members of that clade but not in the outgroup. It is more informative than symplesiomorphy because a symplesiomorphy is a character inherited from a remote common ancestor shared by many taxa (e.g., vertebral column in all vertebrates does not help distinguish mammals from reptiles). A synapomorphy is diagnostic for a specific node (clade) in the tree — it unites only the taxa that inherited it from their most recent common ancestor. (ii) Cladogram from matrix: Species A has no derived characters → outgroup (the ancestral state reference). Character 1 is shared by B, C, D, E → groups B+C+D+E as a clade (sister to A). Character 2 shared by C, D, E → groups C+D+E as a nested clade. Character 3 shared by D, E → groups D+E as sister. Character 4 only in E → autapomorphy of E. Cladogram: A is outgroup; sister group = (B + (C + (D + E))). Most parsimonious tree requires 4 evolutionary events (one for each character, each evolving once). (iii) Most parsimonious means the tree that requires the fewest evolutionary changes (fewest independent gains or losses of characters) to explain the data. Parsimony is preferred because it minimizes ad hoc hypotheses; Occam's razor — the simplest explanation (fewest events) is the best starting hypothesis; convergent evolution (homoplasy) is relatively rare, so the tree requiring the fewest evolutionary steps is most likely to reflect true evolutionary history. 1 pt for synapomorphy definition + cladogram topology; 1 pt for parsimony explanation.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Define synapomorphy; construct cladogram from matrix; explain parsimony.
rubric.minimum_fix: Synapomorphy = shared derived character at a node. More informative than symplesiomorphy (ancestral, too broadly shared). Cladogram: A=outgroup; (B,(C,(D,E))). Each character evolved once → 4 total steps → most parsimonious. Parsimony: fewest evolutionary changes = most likely tree; minimizes ad hoc convergences.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Molecular basis of clock: the molecular clock reflects the accumulation of neutral mutations (mutations that do not affect fitness) at a rate determined by the mutation rate of DNA replication. Because neutral mutations are not subject to natural selection (neither advantageous nor deleterious), their accumulation rate is primarily determined by the neutral mutation rate (errors per nucleotide per generation) × generation time, both of which are relatively stable within a lineage. Genetic drift is the primary force fixing neutral alleles; fixation rate of neutral alleles = neutral mutation rate (by drift theory). Therefore sequences diverge at an approximately constant rate per unit time for neutral sites. (ii) Human-Gorilla calculation: Calibration from known pairs: Human-Chimp: 2.5% / 6 Mya midpoint = ~0.42%/Mya; Rhesus-Baboon: 5.4% / 11 Mya midpoint = ~0.49%/Mya. Using the provided conversion: 1% divergence ≈ 2 Mya. Human-Gorilla: 2.1% × 2 Mya/1% = 4.2 Mya. Estimated divergence: ~4.2 million years ago. (Actual data supports ~6-8 Mya; students should use the provided calibration, not outside knowledge.) (iii) Two limitations: (1) Generation time effect: organisms with shorter generation times have higher absolute mutation rates per year (more cell divisions per year → more replication errors). A mouse molecular clock runs faster than an elephant's. (2) Natural selection affects rate: protein-coding regions under strong purifying selection accumulate synonymous mutations faster than nonsynonymous → clock rates vary by functional constraint. Genes under positive selection accumulate changes faster in some lineages than others. Also: variation in DNA repair efficiency, metabolic rate (oxidative damage), and substitution rate heterogeneity among sites. Any two valid reasons accepted. 1 pt for neutral mutation rate explanation; 1 pt for calculation + 2 limitations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain molecular clock mechanism; calculate Human-Gorilla divergence; describe two limitations.
rubric.minimum_fix: Clock mechanism: neutral mutations accumulate by drift at rate = neutral mutation rate; constant per unit time because no selection acts. Human-Gorilla: 2.1% × 2 Mya/% = ~4.2 Mya. Limitations: (1) generation time effect (short-generation organisms run clock faster); (2) purifying selection slows rate in conserved genes; positive selection speeds it locally.

rubric.evidence_requirements: (i) Homoplasy: analogous structures evolve independently in unrelated lineages due to similar selective pressures (convergent evolution) or can be lost in parallel. In morphological phylogenetics, if two unrelated species share an analogous structure (not inherited from common ancestor), a morphological analysis treating it as a synapomorphy would incorrectly group them together. Example: wings evolved independently in birds, bats, and insects — a morphological analysis using "wings" as a character would incorrectly cluster these groups as close relatives. Streamlined body shape evolved independently in dolphins, sharks, and ichthyosaurs. (ii) Molecular phylogenies more reliable: DNA sequences have far more characters (billions of nucleotide positions) than morphological characters (dozens to hundreds), reducing the impact of any single homoplastic character; synonymous nucleotide changes at 3rd codon positions are nearly neutral and abundant → better molecular clock; molecular data allows statistical methods (maximum likelihood, Bayesian) that model the probability of change at each site and correct for multiple hits (saturation). Specific example: traditional morphology grouped birds with reptiles (classifying them separately as "Reptilia" + "Aves"); molecular phylogenetics conclusively showed birds ARE reptiles — specifically the sister group to crocodilians (archosaurs). Another example: traditional morphology placed whales with other aquatic animals; molecular data shows whales are most closely related to even-toed ungulates (hippopotamus is the closest living relative). 1 pt for homoplasy misleading mechanism; 1 pt for molecular reliability + specific example.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how homoplasy misleads morphological phylogenies; explain molecular reliability; give example of overturned phylogeny.
rubric.minimum_fix: Homoplasy: analogous structures evolve independently (wings in birds/bats/insects); morphological analysis treats as synapomorphy → incorrect grouping. Molecular more reliable: many more characters; statistical models; neutral sites. Example: birds (Aves) are nested within Reptilia with crocodilians as sister — molecular overturned the traditional bird/reptile division. Or: whales sister to hippos.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Three lines of evidence: (1) Genetic/molecular: sequence DNA from both populations (multiple loci — mitochondrial DNA, nuclear microsatellites, or whole-genome SNPs). Calculate FST (genetic differentiation index) between populations. High FST (>0.25) suggests strong genetic isolation; distinct alleles fixed in each population → distinct evolutionary lineages. Species-level divergence may show fixed differences at multiple loci; subspecies would show partial differentiation. Phylogenetic species concept: if populations are monophyletic (each is a clade with respect to the other), they qualify as separate species. (2) Morphological: measure multiple quantitative morphological traits (body size, skull dimensions, pelage color/pattern). Test for statistical differences between populations. Greater and more consistent morphological divergence supports species status; slight average differences support subspecies. Identify diagnostic characters (characters that are 100% fixed as different between populations). (3) Behavioral/reproductive isolation (common garden or contact zone): if the populations are allopatric, identify contact zones where the ranges meet (or create in the lab). Test whether individuals recognize, court, and mate with individuals from the other population. Use acoustic, chemical, and visual cue experiments. If females show significant mate preference for conspecifics, reproductive isolation is evolving → species. If free interbreeding occurs in contact zones, they are likely subspecies. 1 pt per two evidence types with correct reasoning, max 2 pts.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe three lines of evidence for species vs. subspecies determination.
rubric.minimum_fix: Three evidence types: (1) Genetic: FST, fixed allele differences, phylogenetic monophyly; (2) Morphological: diagnostic fixed morphological characters; (3) Behavioral/reproductive isolation: mate preference experiments or contact zone interbreeding. Higher divergence and isolation → species; partial divergence → subspecies.

items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Figure 1 shows the results of a morphological analysis of five species (A–E). Shared derived characters (synapomorphies) are listed in the matrix.
    (i) Define synapomorphy and explain why it is more informative for constructing phylogenies than symplesiomorphy (a shared ancestral character).
    (ii) Using the character matrix data, construct the most parsimonious cladogram for species A–E. Identify the outgroup and explain your reasoning.
    (iii) Explain what "most parsimonious" means in phylogenetic analysis, and why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.

(b) The molecular clock hypothesis proposes that DNA sequences accumulate mutations at an approximately constant rate over time.
    (i) Explain the molecular basis for the molecular clock — why do neutral mutations accumulate at a relatively constant rate?
    (ii) Cytochrome b is commonly used as a molecular clock gene. Table 1 shows the percentage sequence differences in cytochrome b between pairs of primate species, and known fossil divergence dates for two of the pairs. Use the data to estimate the divergence time for the third pair (Human–Gorilla) and show your work.
    (iii) Describe TWO reasons why the molecular clock is not perfectly constant and can give inaccurate divergence estimates.

(c) Convergent evolution can mislead phylogenetic analysis based on morphology.
    (i) Explain how analogous structures (homoplasy) can cause morphological phylogenies to incorrectly group unrelated organisms together.
    (ii) Explain why molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable than morphological phylogenies for resolving deep evolutionary relationships. Give a specific example of a case where molecular data overturned a morphologically derived phylogeny.

(d) A researcher wants to determine whether two geographically isolated populations of mice are separate species or subspecies. Describe THREE lines of evidence the researcher could collect and explain how each line of evidence would contribute to a decision.

synthetic_responses.student_response:
(a)(i) A synapomorphy is a shared derived character that evolved in the common ancestor of a clade and unites only the members of that clade, whereas a symplesiomorphy is an ancestral character shared broadly by many taxa and does not help distinguish a specific clade, making synapomorphies far more informative for building phylogenies. (ii) Species A lacks all four derived characters, so it is the outgroup; character 1 groups B, C, D, and E together; character 2 nests C, D, and E within that group; character 3 nests D and E further; and character 4 is unique to E, giving the topology A as outgroup with B sister to the clade containing C sister to (D, E). (iii) The most parsimonious tree is the one requiring the fewest evolutionary changes to explain the character data, which is preferred because it avoids unnecessary assumptions of convergent evolution and because true convergence (homoplasy) is relatively rare, so the simplest explanation is the most likely to reflect actual evolutionary history.
(b)(i) The molecular clock reflects the steady accumulation of neutral mutations, which are not acted on by natural selection and are fixed by genetic drift at a rate approximately equal to the neutral mutation rate, so sequence divergence accumulates at a roughly constant rate over time. (ii) Using the calibration that 1% divergence corresponds to about 2 million years, the 2.1% divergence between human and gorilla cytochrome b sequences corresponds to an estimated divergence time of about 4.2 million years ago. (iii) The clock is not perfectly constant because organisms with shorter generation times undergo more replication cycles per year and accumulate mutations faster, and because natural selection, whether purifying or positive, can slow or speed up the substitution rate in different genes or lineages compared to a purely neutral expectation.
(c)(i) Homoplasy occurs when analogous structures evolve independently in unrelated lineages due to similar selective pressures, and if a morphological analysis mistakenly treats such a convergent trait as a synapomorphy, it will incorrectly group the unrelated organisms together, as would happen if wings were used to group birds, bats, and insects as close relatives. (ii) Molecular phylogenies are generally more reliable because DNA sequences provide far more independent characters than morphology and can be analyzed with statistical models that account for multiple substitutions at a site, and a well known example is that molecular data revealed birds are nested within reptiles as the sister group to crocodilians, overturning the traditional morphological division between Reptilia and Aves.
(d) The researcher could sequence DNA from both populations at multiple loci and calculate FST to assess genetic differentiation, since a high FST with fixed allele differences would support species status while partial differentiation would support subspecies status. The researcher could also measure multiple morphological traits for statistically significant and consistent differences, looking for diagnostic characters that are completely fixed between the populations. Finally, the researcher could test for reproductive isolation directly, such as through mate-choice experiments or observing behavior at a contact zone, since strong mate preference for conspecifics or lack of interbreeding would support species status while free interbreeding would suggest subspecies.

(a) A synapomorphy is a derived trait shared by a group, which is more useful than an ancestral trait shared by everyone because it actually helps define smaller groups. Based on the character matrix, species A would be the outgroup since it doesn't have any of the derived traits, and the others nest in order from B through E. The most parsimonious tree is the one that needs the fewest changes to explain the data.
(b) The molecular clock works because mutations that don't affect fitness build up at a steady rate over time. Using the given ratio, I calculated Human-Gorilla divergence at around 4.2 million years ago. The clock isn't perfectly constant because different species reproduce at different rates and selection can affect how fast changes accumulate.
(c) Homoplasy is when unrelated species evolve similar traits independently, which can trick a morphological analysis into grouping them together incorrectly, like with wings. Molecular data is usually considered more trustworthy since there's so much more of it to compare, and it's helped scientists figure out relationships that morphology got wrong, like with birds and reptiles.
(d) The researcher could compare DNA between the two populations to see how different they are genetically. They could also look at physical traits to see if there are consistent differences. And they could see if the two populations would actually mate with each other if given the chance.

(b) The molecular clock is based on mutations building up over time at a constant rate, but I'm not confident in my Human-Gorilla calculation.
(c) Homoplasy can make unrelated species look related if they evolved similar traits separately.
