rubric.minimum_fix: At 35°C, water vapor pressure inside the leaf is higher relative to the air, increasing the gradient that drives water loss through stomata.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States guard cells take up K+ (and water follows by osmosis), becoming turgid and bowing open the stoma; losing K+ causes stomata to close.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how guard cells control transpiration by opening and closing stomata.
rubric.minimum_fix: Guard cells accumulate K+, water follows by osmosis, they become turgid and bow apart opening the stoma; K+ loss reverses this.

items.stem: A student investigates whether temperature affects the rate of transpiration in a plant by measuring water loss at 20°C and 35°C.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Transpiration rate is higher at 35°C than at 20°C because the higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, raising the vapor pressure inside the leaf relative to the surrounding air and creating a steeper gradient that drives more water loss through the stomata. Guard cells regulate this process by actively taking up potassium ions, which causes water to follow by osmosis; as the guard cells become turgid, they bow apart and open the stomatal pore, while a loss of potassium reverses this and causes the stomata to close.

Transpiration is higher at 35°C simply because the plant's cells expand more in the heat, which physically stretches the leaf surface and creates more openings for water to escape. Guard cells control the stomata by contracting like a muscle whenever the plant senses it is getting too hot outside, which forces the stomata to close and stop water loss.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fossil fuels store carbon removed from the atmosphere long ago; burning them releases ancient CO2 faster than natural processes can remove it.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle.
rubric.minimum_fix: Combustion of fossil fuels converts long-sequestered organic carbon to CO2, rapidly adding carbon to the atmosphere beyond natural cycling rates.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States CO2 is a greenhouse gas; it absorbs outgoing infrared radiation and re-radiates it back to Earth's surface, raising temperature.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the increase in atmospheric CO2 affects global temperature.
rubric.minimum_fix: CO2 absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth and re-emits it back, trapping heat in the atmosphere and raising global temperatures.

items.stem: A biologist studies the carbon cycle and notes that burning fossil fuels releases CO2 that was sequestered millions of years ago.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle because it releases carbon that was removed from the atmosphere and stored underground millions of years ago, adding it back as CO2 far faster than natural processes like photosynthesis and ocean absorption can remove it. This increase in atmospheric CO2 raises global temperature because CO2 is a greenhouse gas that absorbs outgoing infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emits it back downward, trapping heat in the atmosphere.

Burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle because it destroys carbon atoms completely, permanently removing them from Earth's ecosystems and reducing the amount of carbon available for living things to use. The increase in CO2 raises global temperature because CO2 directly heats up when it touches sunlight, similar to how a dark surface gets hot in the sun.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States Rhizobium receives carbohydrates (energy) from the plant; the plant receives fixed nitrogen (NH3/NH4+) it could not otherwise use.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mutualistic relationship between Rhizobium and legumes in terms of what each partner gains.
rubric.minimum_fix: Rhizobium receives sugars from the plant for energy; the plant gains fixed nitrogen (NH4+) from Rhizobium, which plants cannot make.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States most organisms cannot use N2 directly; nitrogen fixation converts it to bioavailable forms (NH4+, NO3-) needed for amino acids and nucleotides.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why nitrogen fixation is important for ecosystems, given that N2 makes up 78% of the atmosphere.
rubric.minimum_fix: N2 is unusable by most organisms; fixation converts it to NH4+ that plants can absorb for building proteins and nucleic acids.

items.stem: Researchers find that a mutualistic relationship between nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) and legume plants increases soil nitrogen.

synthetic_responses.student_response: In this mutualistic relationship, Rhizobium bacteria receive carbohydrates from the legume plant as an energy source, while the plant receives fixed nitrogen in a usable form, such as ammonium, that it cannot produce on its own from atmospheric N2. Nitrogen fixation is important because most organisms cannot use N2 gas directly despite it making up 78% of the atmosphere, so converting it into bioavailable forms like NH4+ or NO3- allows plants to build essential molecules such as amino acids and nucleotides.

In this relationship, the plant provides nitrogen gas directly to the Rhizobium bacteria, and in return the bacteria give the plant oxygen to help it photosynthesize better. Nitrogen fixation isn't that important for most ecosystems since plants can already absorb N2 gas straight from the air through their leaves whenever they need it.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the change alters R group chemistry; interactions that maintain 3D shape are disrupted, changing the active site or binding surface.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a single amino acid change can cause a protein to lose its function.
rubric.minimum_fix: A different R group changes the chemical interactions holding the protein's shape; if the active site is altered, the protein cannot bind substrate.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States primary structure is directly altered (sequence changes); this ripples into tertiary and quaternary by disrupting folding interactions.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the level of protein structure most directly affected by changing one amino acid and explain why.
rubric.minimum_fix: Primary structure is directly altered; since tertiary and quaternary structure depend on primary sequence, folding is disrupted throughout.

items.stem: A researcher studying protein structure finds that a single amino acid substitution causes a protein to misfold and lose function.

synthetic_responses.student_response: A single amino acid substitution changes the R group at that position, which can alter the chemical interactions, such as hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic interactions, that normally hold the protein's three-dimensional shape together; if this disrupts the active site or binding surface, the protein can no longer bind its substrate properly and loses function. The level of structure most directly affected is the primary structure, since the amino acid sequence itself is changed, and because tertiary and quaternary structure depend on that sequence for proper folding, the effects ripple outward and disrupt the protein's overall shape.

A single amino acid change causes the protein to lose function because it changes the protein's overall size, making it too big or too small to fit into the cell membrane where it needs to work. The secondary structure is most directly affected because that's the level where amino acids are first added onto the chain during translation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States somatic cells are body cells that are not passed to offspring; only mutations in gametes (egg or sperm) are heritable.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a somatic mutation cannot be passed to offspring.
rubric.minimum_fix: Somatic mutations affect only the individual's body cells; gametes are separate and do not carry the somatic mutation.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States proto-oncogene mutation causes overactive growth signals (gas pedal stuck); tumor suppressor mutation removes the brake; both needed to bypass all controls.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how mutations in both a proto-oncogene and a tumor suppressor gene can cooperate to cause cancer.
rubric.minimum_fix: A proto-oncogene mutation drives excess cell division (stuck gas pedal) while tumor suppressor loss removes the brake, together causing cancer.

items.stem: A student observes that a somatic cell mutation in skin cells causes one person's cells to divide uncontrollably but does not affect their offspring.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Somatic mutations occur only in body cells, not in gametes, so they cannot be passed to offspring through egg or sperm; only mutations occurring in the germ line are heritable. In this cancer, a proto-oncogene mutation acts like a stuck gas pedal, causing overactive growth signaling, while a tumor suppressor mutation removes the brake that would normally stop division. Because both the accelerator is stuck on and the brake is disabled, the cell divides uncontrollably.

The mutation can't be passed on because skin cells are too far away from the reproductive organs for the mutation to travel there. Cancer happens because the proto-oncogene and tumor suppressor genes swap functions with each other, so the cell doesn't know whether to grow or stop.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States vaccine contains weakened/killed pathogen or antigen; immune system responds, forming memory cells without causing illness.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a vaccine triggers immunity without causing disease.
rubric.minimum_fix: A vaccine presents antigens from the pathogen; the immune system produces antibodies and memory cells without the harmful effects of the real disease.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States memory B and T cells persist after primary exposure; upon re-exposure, they rapidly proliferate and produce antibodies/cytotoxic T cells.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why the immune response to a second exposure to influenza is faster and stronger than the first.
rubric.minimum_fix: Memory cells created during the primary response proliferate quickly upon re-exposure, clearing the pathogen before symptoms develop.

items.stem: A researcher compares the immune response of a person vaccinated against influenza to one who has never been exposed.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The vaccine introduces a weakened or inactivated form of the antigen, which triggers the immune system to mount a primary response and produce memory B and T cells, without causing the actual symptoms of disease. Upon a real exposure to influenza, these memory cells recognize the pathogen and proliferate rapidly, producing antibodies and activating cytotoxic T cells much faster than during a first exposure, clearing the virus before illness develops.

The vaccine gives the person antibodies directly so their blood already has the antibodies floating around ready to attack the flu virus. The second exposure is faster because the person's body has gotten used to being sick and builds up a tolerance to the virus over time.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the repressor binds the operator (DNA sequence near promoter), sterically blocking RNA polymerase progression.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism by which the repressor protein silences gene transcription.
rubric.minimum_fix: The repressor binds the operator, physically blocking RNA polymerase from moving along the template and silencing transcription.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States inducer binds repressor's allosteric site, changing its shape so it can no longer bind the operator; RNA polymerase can now transcribe.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the inducer molecule reverses repressor-mediated silencing.
rubric.minimum_fix: Inducer binding changes the repressor's conformation, reducing its affinity for the operator; the repressor falls off and transcription begins.

items.stem: Scientists sequence the promoter regions of an inducible gene and find a short palindromic sequence where a repressor protein binds.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The repressor protein binds directly to the operator sequence near the promoter, physically blocking RNA polymerase from moving along the DNA template, which silences transcription. When the inducer molecule binds to an allosteric site on the repressor, it changes the repressor's shape so it can no longer bind the operator; the repressor releases, and RNA polymerase is free to transcribe the gene.

The repressor protein attaches to the RNA polymerase itself and physically covers up its active site so it can't read the DNA at all. The inducer works by breaking down the repressor protein completely, destroying it so transcription can start again.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fungal hyphae extend far beyond the root's reach into soil, dramatically increasing surface area for phosphorus absorption.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how mycorrhizal associations increase plant phosphorus uptake.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fungal hyphae extend into soil far beyond roots, increasing the surface area available to absorb phosphorus from soil particles.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States both partners benefit: plant gains phosphorus (and water); fungus gains carbohydrates; neither is harmed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why this association is considered mutualistic rather than parasitic.
rubric.minimum_fix: The plant receives phosphorus and the fungus receives sugars — both benefit from the relationship, defining it as mutualism.

items.stem: A tropical plant has adapted to very low phosphorus soils by forming associations with mycorrhizal fungi.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Fungal hyphae extend far beyond the reach of the plant's roots into the surrounding soil, dramatically increasing the surface area available to absorb phosphorus from soil particles. This is a mutualistic relationship because the plant receives phosphorus (and water) it could not otherwise access, while the fungus receives sugars produced by the plant's photosynthesis, so both partners benefit and neither is harmed.

The fungus increases phosphorus uptake because its hyphae release acid that dissolves the plant's root cell walls so phosphorus can leak in more easily. This is mutualistic because the fungus is helping the plant, and eventually the plant will give some of its roots to the fungus to use as its own body.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions are channels connecting adjacent cells; ions flow directly from one cell to the next, propagating the action potential.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how gap junctions allow electrical signals to spread between heart muscle cells.
rubric.minimum_fix: Gap junctions create direct cytoplasmic connections; ions (the electrical signal) flow through the channels into adjacent cells without crossing membranes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States gap junctions fail; electrical signals cannot spread uniformly across the heart; uncoordinated contraction (arrhythmia) results.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to heart rhythm if connexin proteins were nonfunctional.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without functional gap junctions, electrical signals cannot coordinate across cells; contractions become uncoordinated, causing arrhythmia.

items.stem: A researcher disrupts the expression of a gene encoding a gap junction protein (connexin) in heart muscle cells.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Gap junctions form direct channels connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent heart muscle cells, allowing ions to flow straight from one cell into the next without crossing the extracellular space, which propagates the action potential rapidly across the tissue. If connexin proteins were nonfunctional, gap junctions would fail, so electrical signals could not spread uniformly between cells, resulting in uncoordinated contractions and arrhythmia.

Gap junctions work like synapses where each cell releases neurotransmitters into the space between cells to signal the next heart cell to contract. If connexins stopped working, the heart would just beat slower because the neurotransmitter signal would take longer to diffuse across the gap.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States zooxanthellae perform photosynthesis inside coral tissue providing sugars; coral provides CO2, nutrients, and shelter.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mutualistic relationship between corals and zooxanthellae.
rubric.minimum_fix: Zooxanthellae produce sugars by photosynthesis that feed the coral; the coral provides CO2 and inorganic nutrients to the algae.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States bleached corals die, eliminating the structural habitat of the reef; many reef species depend on coral structure, reducing biodiversity.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why coral bleaching caused by rising ocean temperatures threatens the entire reef ecosystem.
rubric.minimum_fix: Dead bleached coral loses its structural complexity, eliminating habitat for the diverse fish and invertebrates that depend on it.

items.stem: A biologist studying coral reefs notes that as ocean temperatures rise, corals expel their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) and bleach.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Zooxanthellae living within coral tissue perform photosynthesis and provide the coral with sugars, while the coral in turn supplies the algae with CO2, shelter, and inorganic nutrients, making the relationship mutualistic. When rising temperatures cause corals to expel their zooxanthellae and bleach, the coral eventually dies, eliminating the structural habitat that many reef fish and invertebrates depend on, which reduces overall reef biodiversity.

The zooxanthellae live inside the coral and eat the small food particles the coral catches with its tentacles, while the coral gets nothing back from the algae, so it's actually a parasitic relationship. Bleaching threatens the reef because the white color of bleached coral reflects too much sunlight and raises the ocean temperature even further.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States intermediate birth weights have highest survival; very low (underdeveloped) and very high (difficult delivery) weights have lower survival.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the mechanism of stabilizing selection using birth weight as an example.
rubric.minimum_fix: Intermediate birth weight maximizes infant survival; too low risks underdevelopment and too high risks delivery complications, both reducing fitness.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States stabilizing: mean unchanged, variance decreases; directional: mean shifts toward one extreme, variance may also change.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Contrast stabilizing selection with directional selection in terms of effect on mean phenotype and variation.
rubric.minimum_fix: Stabilizing selection maintains the mean but reduces variance; directional selection shifts the population mean toward one extreme.

items.stem: A scientist studies stabilizing selection in human birth weight, finding that very low and very high birth weights have higher infant mortality.

synthetic_responses.student_response: In stabilizing selection, infants with intermediate birth weights have the highest survival because very low birth weights are associated with underdevelopment and very high birth weights increase delivery complications, so both extremes have reduced fitness. Stabilizing selection keeps the population mean unchanged while decreasing variance around it, whereas directional selection shifts the mean toward one extreme phenotype rather than favoring the middle.

Stabilizing selection happens because doctors intervene more when babies are born at extreme weights, which artificially keeps the average weight the same. Directional and stabilizing selection are basically the same process, just stabilizing selection happens faster over fewer generations.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States founder effect = small group colonizes new area; bottleneck = existing population drastically reduced. Both reduce genetic diversity by chance.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the founder effect and how it differs from the bottleneck effect.
rubric.minimum_fix: The founder effect occurs when a small group establishes a new population; bottleneck reduces an existing population. Both reduce diversity by genetic drift.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States one consequence: low genetic diversity, higher frequency of alleles carried by founders, increased risk of inbreeding.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict one genetic consequence of the founder effect for the island finch population.
rubric.minimum_fix: The island population will have low genetic diversity; alleles that were rare in the mainland population may be common if founders happened to carry them.

items.stem: An island 1000 km from the mainland is colonized by a small group of finches blown off course during a storm.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The founder effect occurs when a small group of individuals colonizes a new area and carries only a sample of the original population's genetic diversity, whereas the bottleneck effect occurs when an existing population is drastically reduced in size; both reduce genetic diversity through chance (genetic drift). One consequence for the island finches is that alleles rare on the mainland could become common if the founders happened to carry them, resulting in an overall population with lower genetic diversity.

The founder effect and the bottleneck effect are the same thing, just with different names, because both involve a population shrinking down over time due to lack of resources. One consequence is that the finches will evolve more quickly to become a completely new species because there is more genetic diversity when a population is small.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States biological species concept = can interbreed and produce viable offspring; if these populations still interbreed they are one species.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain whether these moth populations represent two species using the biological species concept.
rubric.minimum_fix: Under the biological species concept, organisms that can interbreed and produce viable fertile offspring are one species; these populations qualify.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the river prevents migration between populations; without gene flow, each population accumulates different mutations and adaptations by selection and drift.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how the river acts as a barrier to gene flow and could eventually lead to speciation.
rubric.minimum_fix: The river prevents individuals from crossing, stopping gene flow; each population diverges independently until reproductive barriers evolve.

items.stem: Researchers compare two populations of the same moth species separated by a river. They find the populations have diverged in wing pattern but can still interbreed.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Under the biological species concept, populations that can interbreed and produce viable, fertile offspring are considered the same species, so since these moth populations can still interbreed despite the wing pattern differences, they remain one species. The river prevents individuals from migrating between the two populations, stopping gene flow, so each population accumulates different mutations and adaptations independently through selection and drift, which could eventually lead to speciation if reproductive isolation evolves.

These moth populations are already two separate species because their wing patterns look different enough to tell them apart visually, and appearance is what defines a species. The river doesn't really matter for gene flow since moths can fly over rivers easily, so the wing pattern difference must be caused by the environment changing their coloring directly, not genetics.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States GPP = total energy fixed by photosynthesis; NPP = GPP minus autotroph respiration; only NPP energy is stored in biomass available to consumers.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the difference between GPP and NPP and why NPP is more relevant to consumers.
rubric.minimum_fix: GPP is total photosynthesis; autotrophs use some for their own respiration; NPP is what remains as biomass for consumers to eat.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States less light reduces photosynthesis rate; GPP falls and NPP falls; less energy available to support consumer populations.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict how a decrease in solar radiation (e.g., from sediment runoff) would affect NPP in the reef.
rubric.minimum_fix: Less solar radiation reduces the rate of photosynthesis, lowering GPP and NPP, reducing the energy available to support reef animals.

items.stem: A coral reef ecosystem has high primary productivity. Researchers measure gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP).

synthetic_responses.student_response: GPP is the total amount of energy fixed by photosynthesis, while NPP equals GPP minus the energy autotrophs use for their own cellular respiration, so NPP represents the biomass actually available to consumers. A decrease in solar radiation would reduce the rate of photosynthesis, lowering both GPP and NPP, which would leave less energy available to support the reef's consumer populations.

GPP is the energy consumers get directly from eating producers, while NPP is the total energy the producers make before anything is eaten. If solar radiation decreases, GPP would go down but NPP would actually go up because the producers wouldn't need to use as much energy on respiration in the dark.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must list all five: large population (prevents drift), random mating (prevents assortative mating), no mutation, no migration, no selection.
rubric.learner_facing_text: State the five conditions required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and explain what each prevents.
rubric.minimum_fix: Large population prevents drift; random mating prevents unequal partner choice; no mutation, no migration, and no selection prevent allele frequency changes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States natural selection is occurring (differential survival); this violates the no natural selection condition.
rubric.learner_facing_text: A researcher finds that homozygous dominant individuals have higher survival rates. Explain which H-W condition is violated.
rubric.minimum_fix: Differential survival based on genotype means natural selection is acting, violating the no-selection condition of H-W equilibrium.

items.stem: A population geneticist finds that allele frequencies in a large, randomly mating beetle population do not change across generations.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires a large population size to prevent genetic drift, random mating to prevent nonrandom assortment of alleles, and no mutation, migration, or natural selection, since each of these would otherwise change allele frequencies across generations. If homozygous dominant individuals survive at a higher rate than other genotypes, this is differential survival based on genotype, meaning natural selection is occurring and the no-selection condition is being violated.

The five conditions are large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, and no selection, and these conditions exist so the population can keep evolving faster over time toward the fittest genotype. Since homozygous dominant beetles survive more, this means random mating is being violated because the beetles are now choosing mates based on their genotype.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States hemoglobin has 4 polypeptide subunits (quaternary structure); myoglobin has 1 polypeptide (tertiary structure).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the structural difference between hemoglobin and myoglobin.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hemoglobin has four subunits (quaternary structure); myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain with only tertiary structure.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States myoglobin does not show cooperativity and binds O2 tightly at low concentrations; hemoglobin releases O2 at low partial pressures to tissues.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why myoglobin has a higher O2 affinity than hemoglobin at low partial pressures of O2.
rubric.minimum_fix: Myoglobin binds O2 tightly at low concentrations for storage; hemoglobin's cooperativity causes it to unload O2 at the lower partial pressures found in tissues.

items.stem: A researcher compares the structure of hemoglobin in humans and myoglobin in muscle tissue.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Hemoglobin consists of four polypeptide subunits arranged in a quaternary structure, whereas myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain with only tertiary structure. Myoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity at low partial pressures because it lacks cooperativity and binds oxygen tightly for storage, while hemoglobin's cooperative subunit interactions cause it to release oxygen at the lower partial pressures found in respiring tissues.

Hemoglobin and myoglobin have the same structure of one polypeptide chain each, but hemoglobin is found in blood while myoglobin is found in muscle, which is the only difference between them. Myoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen because it's a bigger protein than hemoglobin, so it has more room to hold onto oxygen molecules.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue; without NAD+, glycolysis halts and ATP production stops.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain the metabolic purpose of alcoholic fermentation in yeast.
rubric.minimum_fix: Yeast use fermentation to oxidize NADH back to NAD+, allowing glycolysis to keep running and producing 2 ATP per glucose.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States aerobic respiration uses pyruvate in the Krebs cycle and ETC to produce ~30 ATP; fermentation only yields 2 ATP from glycolysis.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why alcoholic fermentation is less efficient than aerobic respiration.
rubric.minimum_fix: Fermentation only captures energy from glycolysis (2 ATP); aerobic respiration extracts additional energy from pyruvate via Krebs and ETC (~30 ATP total).

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates that when yeast are given glucose in the absence of oxygen, they produce ethanol and CO2 (alcoholic fermentation).

synthetic_responses.student_response: In the absence of oxygen, yeast use alcoholic fermentation to oxidize NADH back into NAD+, which regenerates the NAD+ needed for glycolysis to continue producing ATP. Fermentation is less efficient than aerobic respiration because it only captures the 2 ATP made during glycolysis, whereas aerobic respiration further oxidizes pyruvate through the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain to yield roughly 30 ATP per glucose.

Yeast ferment glucose because fermentation produces way more ATP than aerobic respiration when there's no oxygen available, since the yeast don't waste energy on the electron transport chain. Fermentation is actually more efficient because it makes ethanol and CO2 directly from glucose in one simple step instead of many steps like respiration.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States an insertion shifts the entire reading frame of all codons downstream; a substitution only changes one codon (one amino acid).
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why a single nucleotide insertion is more disruptive than a single nucleotide substitution.
rubric.minimum_fix: An insertion alters the reading frame for all downstream codons, changing every amino acid after it; a substitution only affects one codon.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States the ribosome terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that lacks its C-terminal domain and is likely nonfunctional.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how a premature stop codon resulting from a frameshift mutation would affect the protein product.
rubric.minimum_fix: A premature stop codon terminates translation early, producing a truncated protein that is missing C-terminal sequences and usually nonfunctional.

items.stem: A scientist introduces a frameshift mutation by inserting one nucleotide into the middle of a protein-coding gene.

synthetic_responses.student_response: A single nucleotide insertion shifts the reading frame for every codon downstream of the insertion point, changing all the amino acids that follow, whereas a substitution typically alters only the single codon in which it occurs. If the frameshift creates a premature stop codon, translation terminates early, producing a truncated protein that lacks its normal C-terminal sequence and is usually nonfunctional.

An insertion is more disruptive because it adds an extra amino acid to the protein, making it slightly longer, while a substitution removes an amino acid and makes the protein shorter. A premature stop codon just means the ribosome pauses briefly before continuing to translate the rest of the mRNA normally.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transposase enzyme cuts the transposon from its location and inserts it into a new site (cut-and-paste); or copies itself and inserts the copy.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how a transposon moves from one location in the genome to another.
rubric.minimum_fix: Transposase cuts the transposon out of the DNA and ligates it into a new genomic location, or makes a copy that inserts elsewhere.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States transposon insertion can disrupt a gene's coding sequence or regulatory region, inactivating or altering its expression.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how transposons can cause mutations when they insert into a new location.
rubric.minimum_fix: Inserting into a coding region disrupts the reading frame; inserting into a promoter may silence the gene by blocking RNA polymerase.

items.stem: A scientist discovers a bacterium that produces a toxin by means of a mobile genetic element that can jump between chromosomes.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The enzyme transposase cuts the transposon out of its original location in the DNA and inserts it into a new genomic site, or in some cases makes a copy of the transposon that is inserted elsewhere while the original remains. When a transposon inserts into a new location, it can disrupt a gene's coding sequence or its regulatory region, inactivating the gene or altering its expression and causing a mutation.

Transposons move by being transcribed into mRNA and then translated into a new piece of DNA that attaches itself to a different chromosome using ribosomes. Transposons only cause mutations if they land directly on a start codon; otherwise they just sit in the genome without doing anything.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States: damage causes JA synthesis; JA travels to undamaged cells; binds receptors; activates transcription factors; defense genes expressed.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe the signal transduction pathway from herbivore damage to JA-induced gene expression in a plant.
rubric.minimum_fix: Wounding triggers JA synthesis; JA moves to distal cells, binds receptors, activates transcription factors, and induces protease inhibitor genes.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States JA (or salicylic acid) is transported through phloem to undamaged leaves; those leaves pre-emptively activate defense genes.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how systemic acquired resistance allows undamaged parts of the plant to respond to herbivore damage.
rubric.minimum_fix: Systemic signals like JA travel through the phloem to undamaged leaves, which upregulate defense genes before the herbivore reaches them.

items.stem: A researcher studying plant defense responses finds that jasmonic acid (JA) is produced when a plant is damaged by herbivores.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Herbivore wounding triggers the synthesis of jasmonic acid, which travels to undamaged cells, binds specific receptors, and activates transcription factors that turn on defense genes such as those encoding protease inhibitors. Because JA is transported systemically through the phloem to undamaged leaves, those leaves can pre-emptively activate their defense genes before the herbivore ever reaches them, giving the whole plant a coordinated response.

Jasmonic acid is released into the air around the damaged leaf and undamaged leaves absorb it directly through their stomata to trigger a response. This is not really a systemic response since each leaf only reacts to the JA it senses in the air near it, so the defense is limited only to leaves close to the damage.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States guide RNA contains a ~20-nucleotide sequence complementary to the target DNA; it base-pairs with the target strand, positioning Cas9 to cut.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Describe how the guide RNA directs Cas9 to the correct genomic location.
rubric.minimum_fix: The guide RNA base-pairs with its complementary target DNA sequence, positioning Cas9 adjacent to the PAM site so it can cut both strands.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States tumor suppressor normally halts cell division in response to DNA damage or errors; without it, damaged cells proliferate unchecked.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why disabling the tumor suppressor gene caused tumors to develop in the mice.
rubric.minimum_fix: Without the tumor suppressor, cells with DNA damage or errors cannot be halted or directed to apoptosis, and they proliferate uncontrollably.

items.stem: A scientist uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disable a tumor suppressor gene in mice and observes the development of tumors.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The guide RNA contains a roughly 20-nucleotide sequence complementary to the target DNA, and it base-pairs with that target strand, positioning the Cas9 protein next to the PAM site so it can cut both DNA strands at the correct location. Disabling the tumor suppressor gene removed the cell's ability to halt division or trigger apoptosis in response to DNA damage, so damaged cells were able to proliferate unchecked and form tumors.

The guide RNA works by directly binding to the Cas9 protein and changing its shape so that it becomes attracted to any DNA sequence in the genome regardless of sequence. Tumors formed because CRISPR itself is a foreign protein that the mouse's immune system attacked, causing inflammation that led to cancerous growth.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States photosynthesis rate equals cellular respiration rate; CO2 fixed by photosynthesis equals CO2 released by respiration — no net gas exchange.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain what is happening at the light compensation point in terms of CO2 exchange.
rubric.minimum_fix: At the compensation point, the rate of CO2 fixation by photosynthesis equals the rate of CO2 release by respiration; net exchange is zero.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States plant cannot fix enough carbon to replace what respiration consumes; carbohydrate stores are depleted and the plant eventually dies.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Predict what happens to carbohydrate stores in a plant kept below its light compensation point for an extended period.
rubric.minimum_fix: Below the compensation point, respiration exceeds photosynthesis; the plant consumes stored carbohydrates until reserves are depleted.

items.stem: A researcher measures the effect of light intensity on net photosynthesis rate. Below a threshold, the plant releases more CO2 than it fixes.

synthetic_responses.student_response: At the light compensation point, the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of cellular respiration, so the CO2 fixed by photosynthesis exactly matches the CO2 released by respiration, resulting in zero net gas exchange. If the plant is kept below its compensation point for an extended period, respiration exceeds photosynthesis, so the plant must consume its stored carbohydrates to meet its energy needs until those reserves are depleted.

At the compensation point, the plant stops doing respiration completely and only performs photosynthesis, which is why there's no net CO2 released. If kept below that light level, the plant will just switch entirely to fermentation to make ATP instead of using its stored carbohydrates.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States behavioral (prezygotic) isolation; female frogs recognize only conspecific calls and do not approach other species, preventing mating.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Classify the frog mating call as a type of reproductive isolating mechanism and explain how it prevents hybridization.
rubric.minimum_fix: The species-specific call is a behavioral prezygotic barrier; females only approach males whose call matches, preventing cross-species mating.

rubric.evidence_requirements: Must name one: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, or hybrid breakdown; explains correctly.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Give one example of a postzygotic isolating mechanism and explain how it reduces hybrid fitness.
rubric.minimum_fix: Hybrid sterility is postzygotic: mules (horse x donkey) are born healthy but cannot reproduce, reducing hybrid fitness to zero.

items.stem: Students studying animal behavior observe that male frogs produce species-specific calls, and females approach only males of their own species.

synthetic_responses.student_response: The species-specific mating call is a behavioral prezygotic isolating mechanism because females only approach and mate with males producing their own species' call, which prevents mating between species from occurring in the first place. An example of a postzygotic mechanism is hybrid sterility, as seen in mules produced from horse and donkey crosses, which develop normally but cannot reproduce, reducing hybrid fitness to zero.

The mating call is a postzygotic isolating mechanism because it happens after the frogs have already mated and produced offspring together. A prezygotic example would be hybrid inviability, where the frog eggs are fertilized normally but the call prevents the embryo from developing.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States natural selection is non-random (fit alleles increase); genetic drift is random chance; selection produces adaptation, drift does not.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain how genetic drift differs from natural selection as a mechanism of evolution.
rubric.minimum_fix: Natural selection favors alleles that improve fitness in a non-random way; drift causes random changes regardless of whether an allele is beneficial.

rubric.evidence_requirements: States small samples show more sampling error; chance events change allele frequencies dramatically; large populations buffer these random events.
rubric.learner_facing_text: Explain why genetic drift has a greater effect in small populations than in large populations.
rubric.minimum_fix: In small populations, a single chance event (like one individual failing to reproduce) changes allele frequencies dramatically; large populations buffer random variation.

items.stem: A class simulates evolution by randomly drawing colored beans (alleles) from a jar to model genetic drift in a small population.

synthetic_responses.student_response: Natural selection is a non-random process in which alleles that improve an organism's fitness increase in frequency, while genetic drift is a random process in which allele frequencies change by chance regardless of whether an allele is beneficial. Drift has a much greater effect in small populations because a single chance event, such as one individual failing to reproduce, can dramatically shift allele frequencies, whereas large populations buffer against such random sampling error.

Genetic drift and natural selection are basically the same mechanism, since both cause allele frequencies to change toward whatever makes the population more fit over time. Drift affects small and large populations equally because chance events like storms or disease can happen no matter how many individuals are in the population.
